title: The big groups of life: animals, plants, fungi and microbes, and why scientists keep redrawing the tree of life

summary.text: A mushroom stands still in the soil like a plant, yet it is a closer relative of you than of the grass beside it. How can that be? In this unit you will rebuild a hidden family tree by counting letters, and sort 24 living beings into groups.
summary.art: A mushroom, a tuft of grass and a child's hand side by side on damp soil, with a faint branching line under the ground joining the mushroom to the hand before it joins the grass.

intro.hook: Think of a mushroom, a neem tree and yourself. Which two of the three are the closest relatives? Say what you think, and why.
intro.text: Most people pick the mushroom and the neem tree. Both grow out of the ground, and neither walks about. Scientists thought the same for more than two hundred years, and put mushrooms among the plants. They were wrong. A mushroom cannot make food from sunlight. A mushroom digests food, as you do, and their genes are more like yours than like a neem tree's. In this unit you will find out how anyone can know this. You will also find out why the list of the big groups of life has been rewritten again and again, and why it is still not finished.
intro.art: A child sitting on a step with a mushroom in one hand, looking from the mushroom to a neem tree and then to their own other hand.

outcomes: By the end I can name the big groups of life and say one thing that marks each: bacteria, archaea, protists, fungi, plants and animals.
By the end I can explain the difference between a cell with a nucleus and a cell without one.
By the end I can say why fungi are not plants, and give the evidence.
By the end I can explain how scientists work out who is related to whom from differences in genes.
By the end I can tell how the big groups changed from two kingdoms to five kingdoms to three domains, and what evidence caused each change.
By the end I can say what scientists still argue about: two domains or three, a tree or a web, and where protists and viruses belong.
By the end I can tell a group that is one whole branch of the family tree from a group that people made for convenience.
By the end I can say why most of the variety of life is microbes, and how we know.

terms.meaning: Classification is sorting things into groups by a rule. Scientists classify living beings by who their relatives are.
terms.example: A lion and a house cat are classified together, in the cat family, because they share an ancestor who lived not very long ago.
terms.art: A lion and a house cat sitting inside one drawn circle, with a dog outside it.

terms.meaning: A kingdom is one of the biggest groups that scientists sort living beings into. Animals are one kingdom. Plants are another. Fungi are a third.
terms.example: A crow, an earthworm and you are all in the animal kingdom.
terms.art: Three large circles labelled Animals, Plants and Fungi, with a crow, a coconut palm and a mushroom inside them.

terms.meaning: A domain is a group even bigger than a kingdom. Most scientists count three domains: Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya.
terms.example: Animals, plants and fungi are three kingdoms inside one domain, Eukarya.
terms.art: A tree trunk splitting into three thick branches labelled Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya, with small twigs for animals, plants and fungi on the third.

terms.meaning: A cell is the smallest living unit. Every living being is one cell or many cells.
terms.example: A curd bacterium is one cell. Your body is about seventeen trillion cells working together.
terms.art: A single rod-shaped bacterium beside a patch of many human skin cells fitted together like tiles.

terms.meaning: A nucleus is a bag inside a cell, made of membrane, that holds the cell's genes.
terms.example: Each of your skin cells has a nucleus. A bacterium has none, so their genes lie loose inside the cell.
terms.art: A round cell cut open to show a darker round bag in the middle with coiled threads inside.

terms.meaning: A prokaryote is a living being whose cell has no nucleus. Bacteria and archaea are prokaryotes. The word describes a kind of cell, and it does not name one family.
terms.example: The bacteria who turn milk into curd are prokaryotes.
terms.art: A small rod-shaped cell with a loose tangle of thread inside and no inner bags.

terms.meaning: A eukaryote is a living being whose cells have a nucleus. Animals, plants, fungi and protists are eukaryotes.
terms.example: A yeast is a eukaryote with one cell. A banyan tree is a eukaryote with many billions of cells.
terms.art: A large cell with a nucleus and several smaller inner parts, beside a much smaller bacterium for scale.

terms.meaning: Bacteria are one of the two great groups of living beings whose cells have no nucleus. One of them is called a bacterium.
terms.example: Bacteria make curd, live on your skin and in your gut, and fix nitrogen in the roots of a groundnut plant.
terms.art: A bowl of curd with a magnified circle showing chains of rod-shaped bacteria.

terms.meaning: Archaea are the other great group of living beings whose cells have no nucleus. They look like bacteria under a microscope, but their genes and their cell membranes are very different. One of them is called an archaeon.
terms.example: The beings who make the gas in a gobar gas plant are archaea.
terms.art: A gobar gas tank beside a cowshed, with a magnified circle showing small cells and bubbles of gas.

terms.meaning: A protist is any eukaryote who is not an animal, a plant or a fungus. Protists are not one family. The word is a label for everyone left over.
terms.example: An amoeba, the malaria parasite and a giant brown seaweed are all called protists.
terms.art: An amoeba, a slipper-shaped Paramecium and a strand of brown seaweed drawn together inside a dotted circle.

terms.meaning: A fungus is a eukaryote who feeds by digesting food outside their body and soaking it up. Two or more are called fungi.
terms.example: Mushrooms, the yeast in bread and the green mould on an old lemon are fungi.
terms.art: A mushroom, a slice of bread with small holes and a lemon with a patch of green mould.

terms.meaning: A hypha is one of the fine threads that make up the body of most fungi. Many of them are called hyphae. The whole web of threads is called a mycelium.
terms.example: A mushroom is only the part that makes spores. The rest of the fungus is a web of hyphae spread through the soil or the wood.
terms.art: A mushroom above the ground with a wide web of fine white threads spreading through the soil below.

terms.meaning: Photosynthesis is how plants, algae and some bacteria make sugar from carbon dioxide and water, using the energy of light.
terms.example: A tulsi plant in a pot photosynthesises whenever light falls on their leaves.
terms.art: A tulsi plant in a pot at a sunny window, with small arrows for light, water and air going into a leaf.

terms.meaning: A gene is one instruction in a cell, written as a long string of four chemical letters. The letters are called A, C, G and T.
terms.example: One of your genes holds the instruction for building part of a ribosome. A mushroom has a gene for the same part.
terms.art: A long ribbon printed with the letters A, C, G and T in a row, with one short stretch highlighted.

terms.meaning: DNA is the chemical that genes are made of. A cell copies all their DNA before dividing, and now and then a letter is copied wrongly.
terms.example: The DNA in one of your cells would be about two metres long if it were pulled out straight.
terms.art: A twisted ladder shape unwinding at one end into two strands, each being copied.

terms.meaning: A ribosome is a tiny machine inside a cell that builds proteins by reading a copy of a gene. Every cell of every living being has ribosomes.
terms.example: Scientists compare the gene for one part of the ribosome to work out how a bacterium, a mushroom and a human are related.
terms.art: A small two-part blob with a thread passing through it and a chain of beads coming out.

terms.meaning: A common ancestor of two living beings is an earlier being whom both are descended from.
terms.example: You and your cousin have a common ancestor in a grandparent. You and a mushroom have a common ancestor who lived roughly a billion years ago.
terms.art: Two lines running back from a child and a mushroom and meeting at one small single cell.

terms.meaning: The tree of life is a diagram of how all living beings are related. Each fork in the tree is a common ancestor, and each tip is a kind of being alive today.
terms.example: On the tree of life, the twig for humans joins the twig for chimpanzees before either joins the twig for dogs.
terms.art: A branching tree diagram with a bacterium, a mushroom, a fern, a fish and a child at the tips of different twigs.

terms.meaning: A clade is one whole branch of the tree of life: an ancestor and every one of their descendants, with nobody left out.
terms.example: Fungi are a clade. Protists are not a clade, because the group leaves out the animals, plants and fungi who came from protist ancestors.
terms.art: A tree diagram with one whole branch shaded, from the fork out to every tip on it.

terms.meaning: Horizontal gene transfer is the passing of a gene from one living being to another who is not their offspring.
terms.example: A bacterium can pass a gene for resisting a medicine to a bacterium of a different kind who is next to them.
terms.art: Two different bacteria side by side, joined by a thin tube with a small loop of thread passing through it.

terms.meaning: Endosymbiosis is one living being living inside the cells of another, with both gaining from it. Over a very long time the two can become one being.
terms.example: The mitochondria in your cells are descended from bacteria who began living inside another cell about two billion years ago.
terms.art: A large cell with a smaller bean-shaped cell living inside it, and an arrow to a later cell where the small one has become an inner part.

explanations.concept: Why sort all of life into big groups?
explanations.context: This card explains what the big groups of life are for, and what rule scientists use to make them.
explanations.definition: Classification is sorting things into groups by a rule. Biologists classify living beings by their relatives: two beings are in the same group if they share an ancestor that beings outside the group do not share.
explanations.description: Scientists have named more than a million kinds of living being, and there are many millions more. Nobody can learn them one at a time. A good group lets you learn many facts at once. If you are told that a strange being is a fungus, you already know a lot. You know that they have cells with a nucleus, that they cannot photosynthesise, and that they feed by soaking up food. Why sort by relatives, and not by size or colour? Relatives got their features from the same ancestor, so they share a great many features, including ones nobody has looked at yet. A group made by colour shares only the colour. The biggest groups are called kingdoms, and above them are the domains. They are the first forks in the family tree of all life.
examples: A doctor who learns that an illness is caused by a fungus knows at once that medicines for bacteria will not work on it.
A cook sorts by taste and use. Mushrooms sit with the vegetables in a market, and that is a good sort for cooking.
A biologist sorts by relatives. In that sort, the mushroom sits nearer to the fish than to the brinjal.
explanations.art: A market stall with mushrooms among the vegetables, beside a small tree diagram where the mushroom's twig joins a fish's twig before a brinjal's.

explanations.context: This card is about the oldest way of sorting all life, into plants and animals, and why it lasted so long.
explanations.definition: The two-kingdom system sorts every living being as either a plant or an animal. A being who stays in one place and does not eat is a plant. A being who moves about and eats is an animal.
explanations.description: The Greek thinker Aristotle sorted life this way about 2,300 years ago. In 1735 the Swedish naturalist Carl Linnaeus built his great catalogue of nature on the same two kingdoms of living beings. The system lasted because it fitted everything people could see. A banyan stays still and a goat walks. Mushrooms were put with the plants, because they grow out of the ground and do not move. Corals and sponges were argued over for centuries. The trouble began in the 1670s. Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, a cloth merchant in the Netherlands, made small strong lenses and looked at pond water. He saw tiny beings swimming in it. Later, people found that some of these tiny beings are green and make food from light like a plant, and also swim like an animal. The two boxes had no place for them.
examples: Euglena is a single green cell who lives in ponds. In light they photosynthesise. They also swim with a whip-like tail, and in the dark they can take in food.
A sponge never moves from their rock, so for a long time people called sponges plants. A sponge eats tiny bits of food from the water, and sponges are animals.
Bacteria were first put with the plants, mainly because they did not look like animals.
explanations.art: An old page with two columns headed Plants and Animals, and a small green swimming cell with a tail drawn on the line between them.

explanations.concept: Cells with a nucleus and cells without one
explanations.context: This card explains the biggest difference in build between living beings: whether their cells have a nucleus.
explanations.definition: A eukaryote is a living being whose cells keep their genes inside a nucleus. A prokaryote is a living being whose cell has no nucleus, so the genes lie loose inside the cell.
explanations.description: A cow and a coconut palm look very different. Under a microscope their cells are built on the same plan. Each cell has a nucleus, and each has mitochondria, the parts that release energy from food. A bacterium is built on a different plan. Their cell is usually about ten times narrower, with no nucleus and no mitochondria. The French biologist Edouard Chatton gave the two plans their names in the 1920s. In 1962 Roger Stanier and Cornelis van Niel used pictures from the new electron microscope to show how deep the difference goes. So the widest gap in the living world is not between a plant and an animal. It is between cells with a nucleus and cells without one. 'Prokaryote' describes how a cell is built. It does not name one family, as the card on archaea shows.
examples: A yeast is a single cell, yet a yeast has a nucleus. So a yeast is built more like one of your cells than like a bacterium.
The bacteria in curd have no nucleus. Each one is a few thousandths of a millimetre long.
An amoeba is one cell with a nucleus, and can be a hundred times as long as a bacterium.
explanations.art: A large cell with a labelled nucleus beside a small rod-shaped cell with a loose tangle of thread inside, drawn to the same scale.

explanations.concept: Fungi: a kingdom of their own
explanations.context: This card explains what a fungus is, and the evidence that fungi are not plants.
explanations.definition: A fungus is a eukaryote who feeds by letting digesting juices out onto their food and soaking up the digested food through their cell walls. Mushrooms, moulds and yeasts are fungi.
explanations.description: A plant makes sugar from air and water by photosynthesis. A fungus cannot do this. Fungi have no chlorophyll, the green chemical that catches light. A fungus needs food that some other being has made, as an animal does. But a fungus does not swallow. Most fungi are a web of fine threads called hyphae, which grow through wood, soil, fruit or bread. The hyphae let out juices that digest the food around them, and then soak up the result. Fungi differ from plants in what they are built of, too. Plant cell walls are made of cellulose. Fungus cell walls are made of chitin, the same tough material as the shell of a crab or a beetle. Plants store spare food as starch. Fungi store it as glycogen, as your liver does. In 1969 the American scientist Robert Whittaker gave fungi a kingdom of their own. In 1993 gene studies showed something more: fungi and animals are each other's closest relatives.
examples: A mushroom farmer grows oyster mushrooms on wet paddy straw. The straw is the food. The straw gets lighter and softer as the fungus digests it.
Bread mould grows well inside a dark cupboard, because a mould does not feed on light.
Iodine turns a cut potato blue-black, because potato cells are full of starch. A slice of mushroom has no starch to stain.
explanations.art: A cut-away of a log with a mushroom on top and a web of white threads running through the wood, with small droplets leaving the thread tips.

explanations.concept: Plants and animals, looked at again
explanations.context: This card gives the scientists' meaning of 'plant' and 'animal', which is narrower than the everyday meaning.
explanations.definition: Plants are the branch of eukaryotes whose cells have chloroplasts for photosynthesis and walls of cellulose: the land plants and their closest relatives, the green algae. Animals are the branch of many-celled eukaryotes whose cells have no walls and who feed by taking other beings, or parts of them, into their bodies.
explanations.description: In everyday talk, a plant is anything green that stays still, and an animal is anything that moves. The scientists' groups are branches of the family tree. A chloroplast is the green part inside a plant cell where photosynthesis happens. Chloroplasts are descended from bacteria who once lived free, as a later card explains. Red seaweeds share that same old event, and many scientists count them as plants in a wide sense. Brown seaweeds, such as kelp, got their chloroplasts in a different way and are not plants. Animals are easier. All animals come from one ancestor. Most animals move at some stage of life, but not all. A coral stays fixed to the reef all their adult life and is fully an animal. Humans are animals, on the same twig as the other apes.
examples: Moss on a wet wall and a mango tree are both plants. They share an ancestor who was a green alga.
A sponge, a coral, a butterfly, a gecko and you are all animals.
Sargassum, a brown seaweed that washes up on Indian beaches, looks like a plant and is not one.
explanations.art: A mossy wall and a mango tree on one side, and a coral, a butterfly and a child on the other, with a brown seaweed lying apart from both.

explanations.concept: Protists: the group of everyone left over
explanations.context: This card explains the word 'protist', and why protists are not one family.
explanations.definition: A protist is any eukaryote who is not an animal, a plant or a fungus. Most protists are single cells, but some, such as the giant seaweeds, have many cells.
explanations.description: In 1866 the German biologist Ernst Haeckel made a third kingdom, Protista, for the small beings who were neither plant nor animal. The name is still used, and it is useful. But it is a label for leftovers, not a branch of the tree. Think of sorting your class into the cricket team, the kho-kho team and 'everyone else'. The children in 'everyone else' do not share anything. Protists are like that. An amoeba is a closer relative of you than of a seaweed. A kelp is a closer relative of the glassy single cells called diatoms than of any plant. The eukaryote part of the tree has many big branches, and animals, plants and fungi are only three of them. All the other branches are called protists. Protists matter a great deal. Tiny algae and bacteria in the sea do about half of all the photosynthesis on Earth.
examples: The malaria parasite, Plasmodium, is a protist. In 1897, in Secunderabad, Ronald Ross found the parasite inside a mosquito.
A slime mould creeps over rotting wood like a fungus. Slime moulds are relatives of amoebae.
Water moulds rot potato plants and look just like fungi. Their genes show that they are relatives of the brown seaweeds.
explanations.art: A tree diagram of eukaryotes with many branches, three of them labelled Animals, Fungi and Plants, and all the other branches enclosed by one dotted line labelled Protists.

explanations.concept: Bacteria and archaea: two kinds of cell without a nucleus
explanations.context: This card explains how one group, 'the bacteria', turned out to be two groups as different as a bacterium is from you.
explanations.definition: Bacteria and Archaea are two separate domains of life. The cells of both have no nucleus. They differ in their genes, in the fats that make their cell membranes, and in how they read their genes.
explanations.description: Until 1977, every cell without a nucleus was called a bacterium. Then the American scientist Carl Woese and his co-worker George Fox compared one gene, for a part of the ribosome, across many microbes. The microbes who make methane gas did not match the other bacteria at all. They were as different from bacteria as bacteria are from us. Woese called them a third form of life, now named Archaea. Later work found more differences. The membrane round an archaeon is built from a different kind of fat. The machinery an archaeon uses to read genes is more like ours than like a bacterium's. Many archaea live where little else can: in boiling springs, in very salty water, and where there is no oxygen. Many more live in ordinary soil, in the sea and in the guts of animals. In 1990 Woese, Otto Kandler and Mark Wheelis proposed three domains above the kingdoms: Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya.
examples: All the methane in a gobar gas plant is made by archaea. So is the methane from a flooded paddy field and from a cow's stomach.
Salt pans in Goa and Tamil Nadu sometimes turn pink. The colour comes from salt-loving archaea, together with a red-orange alga.
Judith Braganca and her students at BITS Pilani in Goa study the archaea of Goa's salt pans.
explanations.art: A pink salt pan with heaps of white salt, and a magnified circle showing small square and rod-shaped cells.

explanations.concept: How scientists read a family tree from genes
explanations.context: This card explains how differences in genes show who is related to whom. The Hidden Tree Test lets you try the method.
explanations.definition: Relatedness is read by lining up the same gene from different living beings and counting the letters that differ. The fewer the differences, the more recently the beings shared an ancestor.
explanations.description: A gene is a long string of four chemical letters. Before a cell divides, the whole string is copied. The copying is very good, but once in a long while a letter is copied wrongly, and the change is passed on. When one group of beings splits into two groups, each group collects changes of their own. So two groups who split long ago differ in many letters, and two who split recently differ in few. To compare a mushroom with a bacterium, scientists need a gene that both have. Every cell has ribosomes, so every cell has the genes for ribosome parts. Those genes change slowly, because most changes would break the ribosome. This is why Woese chose one of them. Why trust genes more than looks? A body's shape can change fast when a way of life changes, and unrelated beings with the same way of life come to look alike. Today, machines read whole sets of genes, and trees are built from hundreds of genes at once.
examples: A dolphin looks like a shark, but the dolphin's genes are far closer to a cow's.
In 1993 Sandra Baldauf and Jeffrey Palmer compared 25 proteins. Animals and fungi came out as each other's closest relatives.
Old splits are hard to read. Over a very long time the same letter can change twice, and one change hides the other.
explanations.art: Three short rows of letters stacked one above another, labelled Human, Mushroom and Neem, with the letters that differ circled.

explanations.context: This card is about a question scientists are arguing over now: did our own kind of cell grow out of the archaea?
explanations.description: In Woese's tree of 1990, life has three main trunks: Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya. The eukaryotes are a sister trunk to the archaea. In 2015 a team led by Anja Spang and Thijs Ettema read genes from mud taken near a deep-sea hot vent called Loki's Castle, between Greenland and Norway. They found archaea with genes that were known only from eukaryotes before. On their tree, the eukaryotes do not sit beside the archaea. They sit inside them, as one branch among the archaea. If that is right, life has two first trunks, and we are an unusual branch of one of them. Nobody had seen these archaea alive. A Japanese team led by Hiroyuki Imachi and Masaru Nobu spent twelve years growing one from sea-floor mud, and reported it in 2020. The cell is tiny and grows long, branching arms. The argument is not over, because very old splits are hard to read, and different genes and methods give different trees.
examples: On the three-domain tree, an archaeon and you are cousins from two sister trunks.
On the two-domain tree, you are descended from an archaeon, and your trunk is a branch of theirs.
On both trees, an archaeon is a closer relative of you than of a bacterium.

perspectives.who: Carl Woese, and scientists who keep three domains
perspectives.explanation: Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya are three separate trunks. Eukaryote cells are so different in build that they deserve a trunk of their own, whatever their exact starting point was.

perspectives.who: Tom Williams, Martin Embley, Anja Spang, Thijs Ettema and others
perspectives.explanation: There are only two first trunks, Bacteria and Archaea. The eukaryotes began inside the archaea, when an archaeon took in a bacterium who became the mitochondrion.
The split happened about two billion years ago. Trees of such old events change with the genes chosen and the method used. More archaea must be found and grown before anyone can be sure.

explanations.art: Two small tree diagrams side by side: one with three trunks from the root, and one with two trunks where a twig labelled 'us' grows out of the second trunk.

explanations.concept: Is it a tree at all? Branches that join
explanations.context: This card asks whether the history of life really has the shape of a tree, where branches only split.
explanations.description: On a tree, a branch can split, but two branches never join. The history of life has joins. The biggest are mergers of whole cells. Each of your cells holds mitochondria, and mitochondria are descended from bacteria who began to live inside another cell about two billion years ago. Plant cells also hold chloroplasts, descended from photosynthesising bacteria called cyanobacteria. The American biologist Lynn Margulis argued this in 1967, and most scientists dismissed the idea for years. Genes later showed that she was right: mitochondria and chloroplasts have a little DNA of their own, and it matches bacteria. So a plant cell belongs to three branches at once. There are smaller joins too. Bacteria and archaea often pass single genes to neighbours of a different kind. This is horizontal gene transfer. In 1999 the biologist Ford Doolittle argued that among the microbes there is so much of it that the base of the 'tree' is really a net.
examples: A gene for resisting an antibiotic can pass from one kind of bacterium to another kind in a hospital drain.
A neem leaf cell has genes from three sources: the cell's own nucleus, the mitochondria and the chloroplasts.
A lichen on a tree trunk is a fungus and an alga living as one body. No single twig on the tree fits a lichen.

perspectives.explanation: For microbes, a tree is the wrong picture. Genes have moved sideways so often that each gene has a history of its own. A web or a net shows this better.
Cells still divide into two, so the history of cells is a tree. A core set of genes, such as those for the ribosome, mostly travels with the cell. The tree is real, with some threads crossing it.
Mergers are not rare accidents on the tree. Living together and joining has been one of the main ways that new kinds of life have come about.

explanations.art: A tree diagram whose lower branches are joined by many fine crossing threads, with two thick lines crossing from the bacteria branch to the eukaryote branch.

explanations.concept: How many kingdoms are there today?
explanations.context: This card explains why different books give different numbers of kingdoms, and which answer your child will meet in later school books.
explanations.description: There is no agreed number. In 1969 Robert Whittaker proposed five kingdoms: Monera (all cells without a nucleus), Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia. The Class 11 biology book used in most Indian schools teaches these five, so your child will meet them again. After Woese, Monera was split into bacteria and archaea, which gives six. A scheme published in 2015 has seven. Many biologists who study protists have stopped using kingdoms for them, and speak of 'supergroups'. Why can they not agree? Two different questions are mixed together. 'Who is related to whom?' has a true answer, even when it is hard to find. 'How big must a branch be to be called a kingdom?' has no true answer. It is a choice, like deciding how many colours there are in a rainbow. Most scientists today insist on one rule. A proper group should be a clade: an ancestor and all of their descendants. Monera and Protista both break that rule.
examples: Whittaker's Monera puts bacteria and archaea together, although archaea are closer relatives of us than of bacteria.
Fungi, animals and land plants are clades, so they survive in every scheme.
A book with five kingdoms and a book with three domains can both be describing the same tree.

perspectives.who: Robert Whittaker, 1969, and many school books
perspectives.explanation: Five kingdoms, sorted mainly by how a being is built and how they feed. It is easy to teach and useful for a first map of life.
Three domains come first. Kingdoms are smaller groups inside the domains, and the old kingdom Monera should go.
Only clades matter. Whether a branch is called a kingdom, a supergroup or something else is a matter of taste, so the count of kingdoms is not a scientific question.

explanations.art: Three notebooks open side by side showing the same tree of life, one divided by coloured loops into five groups, one into three and one into seven.

explanations.context: This card explains why viruses have no place on the tree of life as it is usually drawn.
explanations.description: A virus is a set of genes in a protein coat. A virus has no cell and no ribosomes, and is copied only inside a living cell. The tree of life is built by comparing genes that every cell has, such as the genes for ribosome parts. A virus has none of these genes, so there is nothing to line up. For this reason viruses are left off the tree and are classified by a separate system of their own. There is a second difficulty. Viruses probably did not all come from one ancestor. Some may be very old, and some may be bits of genes that escaped from cells at different times. Whether viruses should count as alive is a separate question, and scientists disagree about it.
examples: The flu virus and the virus that infects curd bacteria share no gene that could show how they are related.
Giant viruses with about a thousand genes were found in 2003. A few scientists proposed a fourth domain for them, and most scientists did not accept it.
Viruses carry genes from one cell to another, so they are some of the threads that cross the tree.

perspectives.explanation: Viruses should be left off the tree of life. They are not cells, they have no single origin, and many of their genes were picked up from the cells they infect.
Some viruses are very old and have their own long history. A full picture of life's history should show them, perhaps as a network drawn around the tree.

explanations.art: A tree of life with small virus particles drawn around it and thin dotted lines from the viruses to several different branches.

explanations.concept: Most of the variety of life is microbes
explanations.context: This card explains why animals, plants and fungi, the life we can see, are a small part of the tree of life.
explanations.definition: A microbe is a living being too small to see without a microscope. Bacteria, archaea, most protists and many fungi are microbes.
explanations.description: For most of the time that life has existed, every living being was a single cell. Life is at least 3.5 billion years old, and one study from 2024 puts the last ancestor shared by all cells at about 4.2 billion years ago. Animals with many cells appear only about 600 million years ago. Microbes have had far longer to branch. In 2016 a team led by Laura Hug and Jillian Banfield drew a tree from the genes of more than 3,000 kinds of being. Nearly all its branches were bacteria and archaea. Animals, plants and fungi together were a few twigs at one side. Many of the bacteria on that tree had never been grown or seen. They were known only from genes found in soil and water. By weight the picture is different. A study in 2018 estimated that plants hold about 450 of the 550 billion tonnes of carbon in all living beings. Bacteria hold about 70. All animals together hold about 2.
examples: A pinch of garden soil holds thousands of kinds of bacteria, and most of them have no name.
About 120,000 kinds of fungi have been named. Scientists estimate that there are between 2 and 4 million.
All living beings use the same four DNA letters and the same code for reading them. This is the main evidence that all life shares one ancestor.
explanations.art: A wide fan-shaped tree of life in which almost every branch is labelled as bacteria or archaea, with one small corner holding tiny drawings of a mushroom, a tree and an elephant.

explanations.concept: Every one of these beings senses and decides
explanations.context: This card is about minds. The big groups differ in how their cells are built, but all of them sense the world and act on what they sense.
explanations.description: A being does not need a brain, or even a nucleus, to sense and decide. A bacterium senses food and swims towards it, and senses poison and swims away. Many bacteria let out a chemical signal and measure how much of it is around. In this way they sense how many neighbours they have, and they change what they do when the number is high. The American scientist Bonnie Bassler showed that bacteria use one signal for their own kind and another that many kinds share. A slime mould is one giant cell. In 2000 Toshiyuki Nakagaki put a slime mould in a maze with food at two ends, and they drew their body back into the shortest path between the two. A fungus sends food through their threads to the places where it is needed. Sensing, signalling and choosing are found on every branch of the tree of life, so they are as old as the first cells. A brain is one way of having a mind, and it is not the only way.
examples: A yeast cell senses the signal chemical of another yeast and grows towards them.
A root tip senses water, gravity and touch, and chooses where to grow.
Glowing bacteria in the sea switch on their light only when they sense that enough of them are together.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study how microbes, fungi and plants behave
perspectives.explanation: Sensing, signalling and choosing are found in every living being. Words such as 'decide' describe what these beings really do, whatever their bodies are built from.
What bacteria, fungi and slime moulds do is automatic chemistry. Words such as 'decide' and 'choose' should be kept for animals with nerve cells.

explanations.art: A yellow slime mould stretched along the shortest path through a small maze between two heaps of oats.

agreed.text: All living beings on Earth are related. They are all descended from one ancestor who lived more than 3.5 billion years ago.
agreed.evidence: Every cell uses the same four DNA letters, the same code for reading genes and the same kind of ribosome. The chance of that happening twice separately is extremely small.

agreed.text: Cells come in two builds: with a nucleus (eukaryotes) and without one (bacteria and archaea).
agreed.evidence: Light microscopes and electron microscopes show the nucleus and the other inner parts in every eukaryote cell, and none in any bacterium or archaeon.

agreed.text: Fungi are not plants. Fungi and animals are each other's closest relatives among the kingdoms.
agreed.evidence: Fungi have no chlorophyll, have walls of chitin and store glycogen. Two gene studies in 1993, and many since, put fungi beside animals.

agreed.text: Archaea are a separate group from bacteria, although both have cells without a nucleus.
agreed.evidence: Their ribosome genes, the fats in their membranes and their gene-reading machinery all differ. Carl Woese and George Fox first showed this in 1977.

agreed.text: Mitochondria and chloroplasts are descended from free-living bacteria.
agreed.evidence: Both have their own small ring of DNA and their own ribosomes, and both divide in two by themselves. Their genes match bacteria, not the nucleus of the cell they live in.

agreed.text: Most of the branches on the tree of life are microbes, and most microbes have never been grown or named.
agreed.evidence: Genes read straight from soil, sea water and mud keep turning up whole new branches, as in the tree published by Laura Hug and others in 2016.

challenging.who: Carl Linnaeus in 1753, and most scientists until the 1960s
challenging.for: Mushrooms grow from the ground, stay in one place and do not swallow food. Fungi have cell walls, as plants do.
challenging.against: Fungi cannot photosynthesise. Their walls are made of chitin and they store glycogen, like animals. Gene studies since 1993 show that fungi are closer relatives of animals than of plants.
challenging.context: This card is about the old idea that mushrooms and moulds are a kind of plant.

challenging.claim: Living beings fall into exactly five kingdoms.
challenging.who: Robert Whittaker, 1969, and many school books today
challenging.for: The five kingdoms are easy to learn. They sort by clear features: the build of the cell, one cell or many, and how the being feeds.
challenging.against: Two of the five are not single branches. Monera joins bacteria with archaea, who are closer relatives of us. Protista is a label for leftovers. The number of kingdoms is a choice, not a finding.
challenging.context: This card is about the five kingdoms taught in many school books.

challenging.claim: Life has only two first branches, and our cells grew out of the archaea.
challenging.who: Tom Williams, Martin Embley, Anja Spang, Thijs Ettema and others, since about 2013
challenging.for: Archaea found in deep-sea mud in 2015 carry genes known before only from eukaryotes. On many gene trees, eukaryotes sit inside the archaea.
challenging.against: Trees of events two billion years old are shaky, and some methods still give three separate trunks. Only a few of these archaea have been grown and watched alive.
challenging.context: This card is about whether there are two domains of life or three.

challenging.claim: The history of life is a web, not a tree.
challenging.for: Bacteria and archaea pass genes sideways so often that different genes give different trees. Whole cells have merged, as mitochondria and chloroplasts show.
challenging.against: Cells still come only from the division of cells, and that history is a tree. A core of genes is seldom passed sideways, and those genes give a steady tree.
challenging.context: This card is about whether a tree is the right shape for the history of life.

challenging.claim: Kingdoms are made by people. Only the branches of the tree are real.
challenging.who: Willi Hennig, a German insect scientist, in 1950, and most classifiers today
challenging.for: A branch exists whether or not anyone names it. But nothing in nature says how big a branch must be to be called a kingdom, a class or a family.
challenging.against: Ranks are still useful for teaching, for laws that protect species and for finding things in a museum. Some scientists say that a big gap in build, such as the nucleus, is real enough to mark a rank.
challenging.context: This card is about whether a kingdom is something found in nature or something people decide.

challenging.claim: Living beings can be sorted by how many senses they have.
challenging.who: The Tolkappiyam, an ancient Tamil grammar, and Jain teachers
challenging.for: It sorts beings by how they meet the world, and it counts grass and trees as beings who sense. Western science took far longer to say that plants sense.
challenging.against: Senses do not climb in steps. A plant senses light, gravity, touch and chemicals, and a bacterium senses chemicals and often light. The count of senses does not follow the family tree.
challenging.context: This card is about a very old Indian way of sorting all living beings, by their senses.

big_questions.q: You can count the differences between your genes and a mushroom's only because they line up. What does it mean that they line up at all?
big_questions.hint: Think about the Hidden Tree Test. Could you have counted differences between two messages that were never copies of one message?

big_questions.q: Who is related to whom has a true answer. How many kingdoms there are does not. Why are these two questions so different?
big_questions.hint: Think of a rainbow. The light is really there. How many colours it has depends on where you choose to draw lines.

big_questions.q: Your cells are a merger of an archaeon's descendants and a bacterium's descendants. So which branch of the tree are you on?
big_questions.hint: Draw the tree with a line crossing from one branch to another. Where would you write your name?

big_questions.q: For two hundred years, almost every expert put fungi with plants. What do you believe today that might be this wrong?
big_questions.hint: The experts were not careless. They trusted what could be seen. What can we still not see?

big_questions.q: Most kinds of life are microbes whom nobody has seen. Does a living being matter less if no one has named them?
big_questions.hint: Think of the archaea in a paddy field. They were making methane long before anyone knew they existed.

big_questions.q: If life is found on Mars or on a moon of Jupiter, would it belong on our tree of life?
big_questions.hint: What would you check first? Think of what all life on Earth shares: the DNA letters, the code and the ribosome.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that mushrooms are not plants? This card tells the true story, and the idea that turned out wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: In 1753 the Swedish naturalist Carl Linnaeus listed the fungi in his great book of plants. Mushrooms grow from the ground and do not move, so they seemed to be plants without flowers. For two hundred years the study of fungi was a part of botany. In 1969 Robert Whittaker, an American ecologist, argued that this was wrong. Plants make their food, animals swallow theirs, and fungi soak theirs up. He gave fungi a kingdom of their own. Even then, most people thought fungi were nearer to plants than to animals. In 1993 two teams tested this with genes. Sandra Baldauf and Jeffrey Palmer compared 25 proteins. A second team, in Mitchell Sogin's laboratory, compared a ribosome gene. Both teams found the same thing. Animals and fungi are each other's closest relatives, and plants are a separate branch.
how_we_found_out.who: Carl Linnaeus, who put fungi with the plants. Robert Whittaker, who gave fungi their own kingdom. Sandra Baldauf and Jeffrey Palmer, and the team of Wainright, Hinkle, Sogin and Stickel, who showed with genes that fungi are nearest to animals.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That fungi are plants. Whittaker showed that fungi feed in a different way from plants. The gene studies of 1993 showed that fungi share a more recent ancestor with animals than with plants.
how_we_found_out.art: An old botany book open at a page of mushroom drawings, with a modern printout of rows of gene letters lying across it.

story.title: The Third Table
story.note: A made-up story. Devika, her mother, Reena Teacher and the science fair are imagined. The mushroom growing is real. Women's groups in Wayanad in Kerala grow oyster mushrooms on wet paddy straw packed in plastic bags. The white growth that spreads through the straw is the body of the fungus. Growers keep the bags in the dark for the first fifteen to twenty days. After that they give dim light, fresh air and a spray of water, and small mushrooms appear about three days after a bag is opened. Oyster mushrooms use dim light as a signal for forming their caps, but they do not feed on light. Green mould is a real pest of mushroom bags. The timing in the story is a little kinder than in real life.
text: On Monday morning Devika carried the bag to school in both arms, the way you carry a baby goat. It was a clear plastic bag as long as her arm, packed tight with wet paddy straw. The straw had gone white all through, as if someone had poured milk into the bag and the milk had set.

Forty bags like this one hung in the shed behind her house in Kottathara. Her mother and ten other women had started the shed two years ago. They chopped the straw, soaked it, steamed it and packed it in layers, with a handful of spawn between the layers. Spawn was grain covered in white fuzz. "That fuzz is the mushroom," Amma always said. "The part we sell is only their fruit."
The science fair was on Thursday. In the school hall, Reena Teacher had set out two long tables with paper signs. One sign said PLANTS. The other said ANIMALS.
Joel was at the plants table with six bean seedlings in coconut shells. Ashwin stood at the animals table with two snails in a jar, looking pleased with himself.
"Mushrooms," said Reena Teacher, reading Devika's label. "Good. Plants table, by the window. They will want the sun."

Devika opened her mouth and shut it again. The shed at home had no window at all. But Reena Teacher had taught science for twenty years. So Devika put the bag at the end of the plants table, where the morning sun came in through the bars. She cut eight small crosses in the plastic, the way Amma had shown her. The mushrooms would come out there. "Three days," Amma had said. "Just in time."

On Tuesday morning Joel's beans had turned their leaves to the window like faces. Devika's bag had done nothing. On the window side the white had gone yellowish, and the plastic was warm under her hand. The straw at the eight crosses was dry and stiff. Near the top there was a speck of green, no bigger than a mustard seed.
She knew that green. Amma threw out any bag that showed it. It was a mould, another fungus, who moved into a bag when the mushroom was weak.
"Maybe they need more sun," said Joel kindly. "Mine love it."
Devika sat down on the floor with the bag across her knees and thought about the shed.

For the first twenty days Amma kept the door shut. She hung wet gunny sacks on the walls. In that dark, the white threads spread out from the grain through all the straw. Nobody gave them light. Nobody gave them anything. And still the bags changed. A new bag was heavy, and the straw inside was tough and gold. An old bag, after three crops of mushrooms, weighed almost nothing. The straw inside came apart in your fingers like wet paper.
So where had the straw gone?
She looked up at Joel's beans. Nobody had given them anything either, only water. They had no straw. They had the window.
"They are not doing the same thing," she said aloud.
"Who?"

"Your beans are making their food. Out of the light. Mine can't do that. Mine are eating." She held up the bag. "This is their food. The straw. They have been eating it for three weeks. The sun is not feeding them. The sun is only drying up their dinner."
Joel looked at the bag with new respect. "So they are animals?"
"They have no mouth." She frowned. "They don't walk. They have no leaves. They are not either one."

She carried the bag to the darkest place in the hall, which was under the plants table, behind the cloth. She begged a steel tumbler of water from the kitchen and flicked water over the eight crosses with her fingers, as Amma did three times a day. She turned the green speck to the wall and hoped. Then she left the cloth lifted by the width of a hand. Amma said the mushrooms wanted a little dim light, to know which way was out, and fresh air to breathe. Light to steer by. Not light to eat.
On Wednesday there was nothing to see. She flicked water, and waited, and did not look at the beans.

On Thursday morning she lifted the cloth. At five of the eight crosses, clusters of grey buttons had pushed out. Each was smaller than a peppercorn. They were crowded together like children at a bus window.
Reena Teacher came by to straighten the signs. Devika showed her the bag under the table. She told her about the dark shed, and the straw that got lighter, and the beans who had only a window.

Reena Teacher was quiet for a moment. "I put them with the plants because that is where my own teacher put them," she said. "And her teacher before her, I expect." She looked at the two signs. "So which table do you want?"
"Neither," said Devika. "Can I have another table?"
They carried in a bench from the corridor. Devika wrote FUNGI on the back of an old chart and propped it up. She put the bag on the bench, in the shade, with the tumbler beside it.
The fair had been open for ten minutes when a small boy from Class 2 arrived at her bench. He was carrying a bowl with a plate on top.
"It's curd," he said. "My grandmother says curd is alive. It is not green and it has no legs. Reena Teacher said to ask you where it goes."
Devika looked at the curd. She looked at her sign. Curd did not grow white threads through straw. She had no idea what curd did.
"Not here, I don't think," she said slowly. Then she turned round. "Joel. Is there another bench in the corridor?"
story.epiphany: For the parent: Devika works out that her mushrooms and Joel's beans feed in opposite ways. The beans make food from light. The mushrooms digest the straw they grow in, which is why the old bags are so light. A being who stands still and has no mouth can still be an eater. So the mushrooms fit neither of the two tables, and a third is needed. Then the curd arrives and fits none of the three. This is the history of classification in small: each time people looked closely at a being who did not fit, they had to add a group.
ask: The mushrooms and the beans both grew with nothing added but water. Where did each of them get their food?
Why did the old straw bags weigh almost nothing?
Devika's mushrooms needed a little dim light. How is that different from the way the beans need light?
Reena Teacher put mushrooms with plants because her own teacher did. Is that a good reason? What would be a better one?
Where would you put the bowl of curd? What would you need to find out first?

A dark shed with rows of white straw bags hanging from the roof and wet gunny sacks on the walls, with a woman spraying water.
A school hall with two long tables under paper signs reading PLANTS and ANIMALS, bean seedlings in coconut shells leaning towards a barred window.
A girl sitting on the floor with the straw bag across her knees, looking up at a row of bean seedlings on the table above her.

roots.context: We have learned how life is sorted into big groups, and how genes show who is related to whom. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the Hidden Tree Test, sister messages differed in 4 letters and cousin messages in 8. You could count those differences only because all four were copies of one first message. The same ribosome gene in a mushroom, a neem tree and you lines up letter by letter in the same way. So each difference between two living beings is measured from something they still share. The fewer the differences, the more recently they were one family.
deep_truth.habit: We use differences to put living beings into separate boxes: plant, animal, fungus, microbe. But a difference in a gene can be counted only between two copies of the same gene. So the differences that separate the kingdoms are also the evidence that the kingdoms are one family.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Hidden Tree Test, a count of differing letters rebuilt a family tree that nobody had shown you. In 1977 Carl Woese did this with a ribosome gene, which every cell has, and found the archaea. In 1993 the same method showed that fungi are nearer to animals than to plants.

three.who_am_i: You are an animal, on a twig beside the other apes. Your nearest kingdom of cousins is the fungi. Every one of your cells also carries the descendants of a bacterium.
three.what_is_life: All life on Earth is one family, more than three and a half billion years old. A bacterium, a mushroom and you read your genes with the same code.
three.what_is_this_world: The living world is one family tree, with some branches that join. The lines between kingdoms were drawn on it by people, and people have moved them many times.

roots.thread: Life on Earth began as one kind of cell. Descendants of that cell became the bacteria and the archaea, and later the cells with a nucleus. From those came every amoeba, mushroom, moss and elephant. The differences between them built up one copied letter at a time. The shared part underneath has never been lost, which is why a gene from a bacterium can still be lined up with yours. The many kinds of life are one life that has kept branching, and has sometimes joined again.

teachings.teaching: This ancient Tamil book sorts all living beings by how many senses they have. Grass and trees have one sense, touch. Snails have two, ants have three, and crabs and bees have four. Four-legged animals and birds have five. Humans have six, with the mind as the sixth.
teachings.link: This is a classification of all life, made in South India more than fifteen hundred years ago. Like the tree of life, it puts a blade of grass and a human on one scale, as beings of one kind. Science now sorts by ancestors and not by senses. It also finds that plants and bacteria have more senses than the old count gave them.

teachings.teaching: All living beings are alike in birth. What sets them apart is what each one does.
teachings.link: Valluvar was writing about people, and saying that nobody is born higher than anybody else. The tree of life says something close to this about every living being. All of us come from one birth, the first cells. The kingdoms differ in what their cells came to do: make food, swallow it or soak it up.

teachings.source: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species, second edition (1860), chapter 13
teachings.teaching: Naturalists had long sorted living beings into groups inside groups, without knowing why that worked so well. Darwin wrote that the hidden bond they had been seeking, without knowing it, was community of descent. The groups are families.
teachings.link: Darwin had no way to read genes. A hundred years later, genes showed the bond directly. It reached further than he could test: to fungi, to bacteria and to archaea.

science.text: All known living beings share one ancestor and read their genes with the same code.
Mitochondria and chloroplasts are descended from free-living bacteria, so branches of the tree of life have joined as well as split (Lynn Margulis, 1967).
Whether cells with a nucleus are a sister branch of the archaea, or grew from inside the archaea.
Whether anything like awareness goes with the sensing and choosing that single cells do. Nobody yet knows how to test this.

other_view.who: Many working biologists, and the philosopher Madhva of Udupi
other_view.view: Many biologists would say that the differences are what matter. A bacterium and a banyan share an ancestor, but knowing that does not help you to treat an infection or to grow a tree. The branches are real and separate now, whatever happened three billion years ago. Most scientists also think that only animals with nerve cells have minds. Madhva, who taught in Karnataka in the thirteenth century, held that difference is real and lasting. Each being is truly different from every other being, and the differences are not a surface over a hidden sameness.

practice.title: Three differences, three samenesses
practice.say: Take one leaf from the kitchen, such as a curry leaf. Hold it in your open hand. Sit still and breathe slowly three times. First, find three ways that you and this plant differ. Say them aloud. Now find three things that you and the plant both do. Both of you are made of cells. Both of you take in water. Both of you read your genes with the same four letters. Close your eyes for five breaths. Which list was easier to find? Which list do you think is longer?
practice.kid: Take a curry leaf or any leaf. Hold it in your hand. Breathe slowly three times. Say three ways you and the plant differ. Now say three things you both do. You are both made of cells. You both take in water. You both read genes with four letters. Close your eyes for five breaths. Which list was easier? Which list is longer?

ask: Your genes differ from a mushroom's in thousands of letters, and match in thousands more. Which tells you more about what you are: the differences or the matches?
People drew the line between plants and animals, and later had to move it. Are there any lines in the living world that people did not draw?
A branch of bacteria joined your branch about two billion years ago and never left. When you say 'my family', how far back do you want to count?
roots.art: A child sitting cross-legged with a single leaf on an open palm, with a faint row of matching letters running between the leaf and the child's hand.

games.title: Which Kingdom? Sort 24 living beings
games.context: This is a card game about the big groups of life. Each card gives clues about one living being. You put your token on the group you think they belong to, then turn the card to check.

printables.title: 24 being cards to cut out (the answer is on the back)

items.f: The bacterium who turns milk into curd. One cell. No nucleus. Feeds on milk sugar and makes acid.
items.b: Bacteria. A cell with no nucleus, with the usual bacterial membrane and genes.

items.f: The blue-green slime on a wet wall. Single cells or chains of cells. No nucleus. Photosynthesises.
items.b: Bacteria. They are cyanobacteria. They photosynthesise, but a cell with no nucleus cannot be a plant. Chloroplasts are descended from their relatives.

items.f: The methane-maker in a gobar gas tank. One cell. No nucleus. Lives without oxygen and makes methane gas.
items.b: Archaea. Every known being who makes methane is an archaeon.

items.f: The pink salt-lover in a salt pan. One cell. No nucleus. Lives in water far saltier than the sea. Membrane made of unusual fats.
items.b: Archaea. The unusual fats in the membrane are a mark of the archaea.

items.f: Baker's yeast. One cell with a nucleus. The cell wall holds chitin. Soaks up sugar.
items.b: Fungi. A yeast is a fungus who lives as single cells.

items.f: An oyster mushroom. Threads of cells with nuclei. No chlorophyll. Digests straw outside their body and soaks it up.
items.b: Fungi. Feeding by soaking up food digested outside the body is the mark of a fungus.

items.f: The green mould on an old lemon. Threads of cells with nuclei. Powdery green spores. Digests the lemon peel.
items.b: Fungi. The green is the colour of the spores. It is not chlorophyll.

items.f: An amoeba. One large cell with a nucleus. No cell wall. Creeps along and wraps round food.
items.b: Protists. One cell with a nucleus, and not an animal, a plant or a fungus.

items.f: A Paramecium. One cell with a nucleus, covered in tiny beating hairs. Swims and sweeps food into a groove.
items.b: Protists. They behave like a tiny animal, but an animal has many cells.

items.f: The malaria parasite. One cell with a nucleus. Lives inside red blood cells and inside mosquitoes.
items.b: Protists. A single cell with a nucleus who lives inside other beings.

items.f: Sargassum, a brown seaweed. Many cells with nuclei. Photosynthesises with golden-brown chloroplasts. A relative of diatoms.
items.b: Protists. A brown seaweed looks like a plant, but is on a different branch from the plants.

items.f: A Euglena. One cell with a nucleus. Has green chloroplasts. Swims with a whip-like tail.
items.b: Protists. They photosynthesise like a plant and swim like an animal, and are on a branch of their own.

items.f: A diatom. One cell with a nucleus, inside a case like glass. Photosynthesises. Floats in the sea and in ponds.
items.b: Protists. Diatoms do a large share of the photosynthesis in the sea.

items.f: A slime mould. One giant creeping cell with many nuclei. Wraps round bacteria and eats them. Makes spores.
items.b: Protists. Slime moulds were once placed with the fungi. They are relatives of amoebae.

items.f: Moss on a damp wall. Many cells with nuclei. Cell walls of cellulose. Green chloroplasts. Makes spores, not seeds.
items.b: Plants. Mosses are land plants who have no seeds or flowers.

items.f: A coconut palm. Many cells with nuclei. Cell walls of cellulose. Green chloroplasts. Makes seeds.
items.b: Plants. A land plant who makes flowers and seeds.

items.f: Pond silk, the green threads in a pond. Threads of cells with nuclei. Cell walls of cellulose. Green spiral chloroplasts.
items.b: Plants, in the wide sense. Green algae are the closest relatives of land plants. Older books call them protists, so either mat scores.

items.f: A sea sponge. Many cells with nuclei and no cell walls. Fixed to a rock. Filters bits of food from the water.
items.b: Animals. A sponge never moves from their rock, but a sponge eats, and has animal cells.

items.f: A coral. Many cells with no cell walls. Sits in a stony cup. Catches tiny animals with stinging arms.
items.b: Animals. Many corals also keep algae inside their bodies, but the coral is an animal.

items.f: An earthworm. Many cells with no cell walls. Swallows soil and digests the dead leaves in it.
items.b: Animals. Many cells, no cell walls, and food taken inside the body.

items.f: A house gecko. Many cells with no cell walls. Has a backbone. Hunts insects on the wall at night.
items.b: Animals. A gecko is an animal with a backbone, a reptile.

items.f: A human. Many cells with no cell walls. Has a backbone. Eats plants, fungi and other animals.
items.b: Animals. Humans are animals, on the same twig as the other apes.

items.f: A lichen on a tree trunk. A grey-green crust made of fungus threads, with green algae living between the threads.
items.b: No single mat fits. A lichen is a fungus and an alga living as one body, so a lichen belongs to two groups at once.

items.f: A flu virus. Genes inside a protein coat. No cell and no ribosomes. Copied only inside a living cell.
items.b: No single mat fits. A virus is not a cell. Viruses are left off the tree of life and are classified separately.

printables.title: 7 mats: write each name on a sheet of paper
One token for each player: a coin, a seed or a button

rules: Lay the seven mats on the table or the floor. Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile with the clue side up. Each player takes a token.
One player reads the top card aloud. Nobody turns the card over yet.
Count to three together. On three, every player puts a token on one mat.
Turn the card over and read the back. Each player on the right mat scores 1 point. A right choice of 'No single mat fits' scores 2 points.
Before the tokens are picked up, a player who was right says which clue decided it.
Play all 24 cards. The player with the most points wins. If you play alone, 18 points or more is a win. Then play again and try to beat your score.
