flow.do: 1. Cut out the 24 cards. 2. Write the seven mat names on seven sheets of paper. 3. Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile, clue side up. 4. Give each player a token.
flow.say: Each card describes one living being. We will decide which big group they belong to, using only the clues.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Write the seven mat names on seven sheets. Shuffle the cards. Take a token.
flow.context: This is the first step of Which Kingdom? Here you make the mats and set out the cards.

flow.do: 1. Read the top card aloud. 2. Count to three. 3. Everyone puts a token on a mat. 4. Turn the card and read the back. 5. A player who was right names the clue that decided it.
flow.say: Ask two things first. Do the cells have a nucleus? How does this being get their food?
flow.kid: Read the clues. Is there a nucleus? How do they get food? Put your token on a mat. Turn the card.

ask.q: A cyanobacterium photosynthesises. Why are they not a plant?
good: Their cell has no nucleus, and every plant cell has one.
They are bacteria. Chloroplasts in plants came from their relatives.

flow.parent: The two questions in the 'say' line settle most cards. No nucleus means bacteria or archaea. With a nucleus, look at how the being feeds and whether they have many cells. Do not correct a wrong token before the card is turned.
flow.context: This is the main part of Which Kingdom? Here you read each card, choose a mat and check the answer.

flow.do: 1. Count the points. 2. Lay out the cards that most players got wrong. 3. Ask what made each one hard.
flow.say: Which cards fooled us? What did each of those beings look like, and what were they really?
flow.kid: Count your points. Find the cards that fooled you. Say what made each one hard.

ask.q: Which mat had the most different kinds of being on it? Why?
good: Protists, because that mat takes everyone who does not fit the others.
Protists are not one family, so they are very mixed.

flow.context: This is the last step of Which Kingdom? Here you count the points and look again at the hard cards.

games.title: Closer Relative? A game of lookalikes and real families
games.context: This is a card game about who is related to whom. Each card names one living being and two others. You choose which of the two is the closer relative, then turn the card to check.

printables.title: 16 pair cards to cut out (the answer is on the back)

items.f: A mushroom. Who is the closer relative: (A) a moss, or (B) a human?
items.b: B, the human. Fungi and animals share a more recent ancestor with each other than either shares with plants.

items.f: Baker's yeast. Who is the closer relative: (A) a mushroom, or (B) a curd bacterium?
items.b: A, the mushroom. Yeasts and mushrooms are both fungi. A bacterium has no nucleus and is in another domain.

items.f: A brown seaweed. Who is the closer relative: (A) a coconut palm, or (B) a diatom?
items.b: B, the diatom. Brown seaweeds and diatoms are on the same branch of protists. Neither is a plant.

items.f: A human. Who is the closer relative: (A) an amoeba, or (B) a neem tree?
items.b: A, the amoeba. Gene trees put amoebae on the side of the tree that leads to animals and fungi.

items.f: A slime mould. Who is the closer relative: (A) a bread mould, or (B) an amoeba?
items.b: B, the amoeba. Slime moulds make spores like a fungus, but their genes place them with the amoebae.

items.f: An archaeon from a hot spring. Who is the closer relative: (A) a curd bacterium, or (B) a human?
items.b: B, the human. Archaea look like bacteria, but they share a more recent ancestor with cells that have a nucleus.

items.f: The water mould who rots potato plants. Who is the closer relative: (A) a bread mould, or (B) a brown seaweed?
items.b: B, the brown seaweed. Water moulds grow in threads like fungi, but they are on the branch of the brown seaweeds and diatoms.

items.f: A sea sponge. Who is the closer relative: (A) a mushroom, or (B) a brown seaweed?
items.b: A, the mushroom. A sponge is an animal, and fungi are the animals' nearest kingdom.

items.f: A cyanobacterium. Who is the closer relative: (A) a moss, or (B) a curd bacterium?
items.b: B, the curd bacterium. Both are bacteria. But the chloroplasts inside every moss cell are descended from cyanobacteria.

items.f: A moss. Who is the closer relative: (A) pond silk, a green alga, or (B) a mushroom?
items.b: A, the green alga. Land plants came from green algae. They share cellulose walls and the same kind of chloroplast.

items.f: A coral. Who is the closer relative: (A) a red seaweed, or (B) a butterfly?
items.b: B, the butterfly. A coral is an animal, though a coral stays in one place like a seaweed.

items.f: A Euglena, a green swimming cell. Who is the closer relative: (A) a moss, or (B) the parasite who causes sleeping sickness?
items.b: B, the parasite. Euglena and that parasite are on the same branch of protists. Euglena's chloroplasts were taken in later.

items.f: The malaria parasite. Who is the closer relative: (A) the bacterium who causes typhoid, or (B) a Paramecium?
items.b: B, the Paramecium. Both are single cells with a nucleus, on the same branch of protists.

items.f: The mitochondria inside your cells. Who is the closer relative: (A) a curd bacterium, or (B) an archaeon?
items.b: A, the curd bacterium. Mitochondria are descended from bacteria who began living inside another cell.

items.f: A red seaweed, the kind used to make agar. Who is the closer relative: (A) a brown seaweed, or (B) a mango tree?
items.b: B, the mango tree, on most gene trees. Red seaweeds, green algae and land plants share the same first chloroplast.

items.f: A dog. Who is the closer relative: (A) a mushroom, or (B) a mango tree?
items.b: A, the mushroom. Every animal is a closer relative of every fungus than of any plant.

printables.title: Score sheet
items: The card that surprised me most: __

rules: Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile with the question side up.
One player reads the top card aloud.
Count to three together. On three, every player holds up one finger for A or two fingers for B.
Turn the card over and read the answer and the reason. Each player who was right scores 1 point.
After all 16 cards, the player with the most points wins. If you play alone, 11 points or more is a win.
Put the cards you got wrong in a pile and play them once more.

setup.art: A pile of question cards on a table, with the top card showing a drawing of a mushroom and the letters A and B.
setup.caption: 1. Put the cards in a pile, question side up.

setup.art: Two children holding up one finger and two fingers at the same moment, while a third child holds a card.
setup.caption: 2. On the count of three, hold up one finger for A or two fingers for B.

setup.art: A card turned over on the table and a child marking a point on a score sheet.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card. Read the answer and the reason.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 16 cards. 2. Shuffle them and put them in a pile, question side up. 3. Agree the signal: one finger for A and two fingers for B.
flow.say: Each card asks who is the closer relative. Looks will sometimes point the wrong way, so think about cells and feeding too.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Shuffle them. One finger means A. Two fingers mean B.
flow.context: This is the first step of Closer Relative? Here you set out the cards and agree the finger signal.

flow.do: 1. Read the top card aloud. 2. Count to three. 3. Everyone shows one or two fingers. 4. Turn the card and read the reason aloud.
flow.say: Before you choose, ask yourself one thing. Am I going by how they look, or by what I know about their cells?
flow.kid: Read the card. Think about cells, not looks. Show one finger or two. Turn the card.

ask.q: A water mould looks just like a bread mould. Why do unrelated beings sometimes look so alike?
good: They live in the same way, so the same shape works for both.
Growing as fine threads is a good way to soak up food, whoever your ancestors were.

flow.parent: Many of these answers surprise grown-ups too. The point is not to remember them. The point is to notice how often a way of life makes unrelated beings look alike.
flow.context: This is the main part of Closer Relative? Here you read each card, choose A or B and check the answer.

flow.do: 1. Count the points. 2. Each player fills in the score sheet. 3. Play the missed cards once more.
flow.say: Which answer surprised you most? What would a scientist have to measure to find that out?
flow.kid: Count your points. Write the card that surprised you most. Play your missed cards again.
flow.context: This is the last step of Closer Relative? Here you count the points and replay the cards you missed.

experiments.title: The Hidden Tree Test: can counting letters rebuild a family tree that nobody shows you?
experiments.context: In this experiment a grown-up secretly builds a small family tree of copied messages, with a few letters changed at each copying. You are given only the four last messages. You count the letters that differ and try to rebuild the hidden tree.
experiments.question: Four beings each carry a message of twelve letters, copied from one first message. Can the number of differing letters show who is whose sister? And if the bodies say one thing and the letters say another, which is right?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Look at the four beings and the bodies drawn on their slips. Which two are sisters, copied from the same parent message? Write your guess and the reason for it. Then guess again: will counting the letters that differ give the same sisters as the bodies do? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every copy gets exactly 2 changed letters, so every line of the family changes at the same speed. A chit is never put back in the tumbler, so no place in the message is changed twice. The person who counts must not see the hidden slips until the tree is drawn. The bodies are given by a fixed rule: one still body and one swimming body on each side of the tree. That is done on purpose, to find out what happens when looks and letters disagree.

materials.item: sheets of plain paper, used on one side is fine
a pencil and an eraser
scissors
a steel tumbler to hold the number chits
a ruler

schedule.what: Make the chits. A grown-up builds the hidden tree. Guess the sisters, count the differing letters for six pairs, draw the tree and compare it with the hidden one.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for all six pairs. Draw the family tree that the numbers give. After the hidden slips are shown, write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.

setup.art: Twelve small paper chits numbered 1 to 12 in a steel tumbler, beside a paper slip with the letters ACGTACGTACGT written in boxes.
setup.caption: 1. Number 12 chits. Write the first message, 12 letters long, on a slip.

setup.art: A grown-up copying a row of letters onto a new slip and changing two of them, with two numbered chits lying beside the slip, while a child looks the other way.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up copies the message. For each copy, two chits say which two letters to change.

setup.art: Four paper slips labelled Being 1 to Being 4, each with a row of twelve letters, two with a small rooted shape drawn on them and two with a small swimming shape.
setup.caption: 3. You get only the four last copies, each with a body drawn on the slip.

setup.art: Two letter slips laid one under the other, with pencil dots under the places where the letters differ, and a child writing a number in a table.
setup.caption: 4. Lay two slips together. Count the places where the letters differ.

flow.do: 1. Your child cuts 12 small chits and numbers them 1 to 12. 2. They put the chits in the tumbler. 3. They cut 7 paper slips, each about 15 centimetres long. 4. They rule a table with three columns and six rows.
flow.say: We are going to make a family of copied messages. First we need twelve number chits, seven slips and a table for the results.
flow.kid: Cut 12 chits. Number them 1 to 12. Put them in the tumbler. Cut 7 long slips. Rule a table with six rows.
flow.parent: The six rows are for the six pairs: beings 1 and 2, 1 and 3, 1 and 4, 2 and 3, 2 and 4, 3 and 4. The column headings are in the results table.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Hidden Tree Test. Here you make the number chits, the slips and the results table.

flow.do: 1. Your child looks away. 2. Write ACGTACGTACGT on a slip and mark it 'First'. 3. Copy it onto two slips, A and B. 4. For each copy, draw 2 chits and change the letters at those two places. 5. Copy A onto two more slips and B onto two more, changing 2 letters each time. 6. Never put a chit back.
flow.say: Look away now. I am copying the message down a family tree, and I change two letters every time I copy.
flow.kid: Working with a grown-up? Look away while they build the tree. Working alone? Copy these four messages onto slips. Being 1: TGGTGTGTACGT. Stands still. Being 2: ACACACGTCAGT. Stands still. Being 3: TGGTACCAACGT. Swims. Being 4: ACACACGTACTG. Swims.
flow.parent: Chit 5 means the fifth letter. Change it to any other of the four letters. You will use all 12 chits: 2 each for A and B, and 2 each for their four copies. Now name the four last slips on the front. Call A's two copies Being 1 and Being 3. Call B's two copies Being 2 and Being 4. On Being 1 and Being 2 write 'stands still' and draw roots. On Being 3 and Being 4 write 'swims' and draw a tail. Hide the slips First, A and B.
flow.context: This is step 2 of 7 of the Hidden Tree Test. Here a grown-up secretly builds the family tree of messages.

flow.do: 1. Give your child the four slips, Being 1 to Being 4. 2. Ask which two are sisters, and why. 3. Ask whether counting letters will agree with the bodies, and why. 4. Write both guesses down.
flow.say: Here are four beings. Two pairs of them are sisters. Which two do you think are sisters? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the four beings. Guess which two are sisters. Say why. Guess if the letters will agree. Write it down.

good: Beings 1 and 2 both stand still, so they look like sisters.
I am not sure the bodies tell us, because the message is what was copied.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Most children pair the beings by their bodies.
flow.context: This is step 3 of 7 of the Hidden Tree Test. This step is for guessing. You guess before you count any letters.

flow.do: 1. Your child lays Being 1 above Being 2, with the letters lined up. 2. They put a pencil dot under each place where the two letters differ. 3. They count the dots and write the number in the table. 4. They do the same for the other five pairs.
flow.say: Line up two messages, letter under letter. Put a dot wherever they differ. How many dots are there for this pair?
flow.kid: Lay one slip under another. Line up the letters. Dot each place where they differ. Count the dots. Do all six pairs.
flow.parent: With the ready-made set, the counts are 8, 4, 8, 8, 4 and 8, in the order of the table rows. With your own tree, two pairs differ in 4 letters and four pairs differ in 8. Rub the dots out between pairs, or use a fresh strip of paper under the slips.
flow.context: This is step 4 of 7 of the Hidden Tree Test. Here you count the letters that differ for each of the six pairs.

flow.do: 1. Ask which pairs have the fewest differences. 2. Your child joins each of those pairs with a small fork on paper. 3. They join the two forks lower down to make one tree. 4. They write the number of differences beside each fork.
flow.say: Which pairs differ least? Join each of those pairs with a fork. Then join the two forks into one tree.
flow.kid: Find the two pairs with the fewest differences. Join each pair with a fork. Join the two forks into one tree.

ask.q: Why should the pair with the fewest differences be joined first?
good: They have had the least time to change since they were one message.
Fewer copyings separate them.

flow.context: This is step 5 of 7 of the Hidden Tree Test. Here you draw the family tree that your numbers give.

flow.do: 1. Bring out the hidden slips First, A and B. 2. Lay all seven slips on the floor as the real tree. 3. Your child compares it with the tree they drew. 4. Explain how the bodies were given.
flow.say: Here is the real tree. Does your tree match? Which was right about the sisters, the bodies or the letters?
flow.kid: Look at the real tree. Does your tree match? Working alone? Beings 1 and 3 are sisters. Beings 2 and 4 are sisters.
flow.parent: Say plainly that you gave one still body and one swimming body to each side of the tree. In real life this happens when relatives take up different ways of life, and when unrelated beings take up the same one.

check.q: Two messages differ in 4 letters. Two others differ in 8. Which pair shared a parent message more recently?
options: The pair that differs in 4 letters
The pair that differs in 8 letters
Nobody can tell from the letters
check.why: The pair that differs in 4. Changes build up with every copying, so fewer differences mean fewer copyings since the two were one message. Choosing 8 mixes up 'more different' with 'more closely related'. Choosing 'nobody can tell' forgets that every copy changed at the same speed.

flow.context: This is step 6 of 7 of the Hidden Tree Test. Here the hidden slips are shown and you compare the two trees.

flow.do: 1. Your child writes three sentences: what they thought, what they saw and why it happened. 2. Ask why counting worked without seeing the parents. 3. Ask what would go wrong if one place changed twice.
flow.say: Write your claim, your evidence and your reason. You never saw the parent messages. So how could the letters show you the tree?
flow.kid: Write what you thought. Write what you saw. Write why it happened. How did letters show a tree you never saw?

ask.q: You could count differences between these messages. Could you count differences between two messages that were never copies of one message?
good: No, because nothing would line up.
You can only count differences from something that started the same.

flow.parent: A strong answer says that each copy carries the parent's changes plus two new ones. So sisters share the parent's changes and differ only in their own. Scientists do this with a real gene that every cell has.
flow.think: Over a very long time, the same place in a gene can change twice. How would that spoil the count?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Hidden Tree Test. Here you write what you found and explain why counting letters worked.

experiments.title: Light or Dark: does a mould need light the way a seedling does?
experiments.context: In this experiment you keep damp chapati and sprouting seeds for a week, some in the light and some in the dark. A mould is a fungus and a seedling is a plant. You find out whether the two need light in the same way.
experiments.question: For two hundred years, fungi were classified as plants. A plant needs light to make food. Does a mould grow less in the dark than in the light? And what happens to seedlings kept in the same dark?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will the chapati in the dark grow less mould than the chapati in the light, the same amount, or more? Will the seedlings in the dark look the same as the seedlings in the light? Write both guesses and the reason for each.
experiments.fair_test: The two chapati pieces are the same size, get the same water and are sealed in the same kind of pouch. The two lots of seeds are the same kind and number, on the same amount of wet cotton. The light set and the dark set stand side by side, so they are equally warm. Keep both out of direct sun, because sun would heat the light set. Change only one thing: light or no light.
results_table: Mould on chapati in the light
Mould on chapati in the dark
Seedlings in the light: colour and height
Seedlings in the dark: colour and height

materials.item: a piece of chapati, roti or dosa about as big as your palm, cut in two (packet bread also works, but can take more than a week)
small clear plastic pouches that seal, or clear polythene bags and rubber bands
methi or mustard seeds
saucers or steel lids, each with a pad of wet cotton wool or folded tissue
a cardboard box or a large steel vessel to turn upside down over the dark set
a teaspoon, water, a ruler and a notebook

experiments.safety: Do not open the pouches once mould has grown, and do not sniff them, because mould spores make some people sneeze or wheeze. At the end, put the sealed pouches in the dustbin. Do not eat the sprouts.

schedule.what: Set up two chapati pouches and two saucers of seeds. Put one of each in the light and one of each under the box. Write your guesses.
Look at all four quickly. Write what you see. Add a teaspoon of water to each seed pad.
Look again and write what you see. Add a teaspoon of water to each seed pad.
Judge the mould on each chapati. Measure five seedlings from each saucer. Write what you found and why.

experiments.record: Fill in the table on days 3, 5 and 7. For mould, write 'none', 'a few specks', 'about a quarter', 'about half' or 'nearly all'. For seedlings, write the colour and the height of five of them. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results on day 7
example_chart.note: These results are made up, to show what a finished table can look like. Yours will be different.

setup.art: Two pieces of chapati, each sprinkled with water and sealed in a clear plastic pouch, lying on a shelf.
setup.caption: 1. Dampen two chapati pieces, leave them open for half an hour, then seal each in a clear pouch.

setup.art: Two saucers, each with a pad of wet cotton wool and about twenty methi seeds spread on it.
setup.caption: 2. Spread 20 seeds on wet cotton in each of two saucers.

setup.art: A shelf near a window with one pouch and one saucer standing in the open, and beside them an upturned cardboard box covering the other pouch and saucer.
setup.caption: 3. Put one pouch and one saucer in the light. Cover the other pair with a box, right beside them.

setup.art: A child holding a ruler beside a tall pale yellow seedling and a short green seedling, with two sealed pouches of mouldy chapati on the table.
setup.caption: 4. On day 7, judge the mould through the pouch and measure five seedlings from each saucer.

flow.do: 1. Cut the chapati into two equal pieces. 2. Sprinkle one teaspoon of water over each piece. 3. Leave them open on a plate for 30 minutes. 4. Seal each piece in a clear pouch. 5. Label them 'light' and 'dark'.
flow.say: Mould spores are floating in the air of every room. We leave the chapati open so that some spores can land on it.
flow.kid: Cut the chapati in two. Sprinkle a teaspoon of water on each piece. Leave them open for 30 minutes. Seal each piece in a pouch.
flow.parent: Do the seed step while the chapati lies open. The chapati should be damp and not dripping. A spore is a single cell that a fungus sends out to start a new fungus.
flow.context: This is the first step of Light or Dark. Here you prepare two damp pieces of chapati and seal them in clear pouches.

flow.do: 1. Put a pad of cotton wool on each saucer. 2. Wet each pad with three teaspoons of water. 3. Spread 20 seeds on each pad. 4. Put one pouch and one saucer on a bright shelf, out of direct sun. 5. Put the other pair beside them and cover them with the box.
flow.say: One chapati and one saucer of seeds get light. The other chapati and saucer get the same warmth and water, but no light.
flow.kid: Wet two cotton pads. Spread 20 seeds on each. Put one pouch and one saucer in the light. Cover the other pair with the box.
flow.parent: The box must touch the shelf all round, so that no light gets in. Lift it only to look and to add water.
flow.context: This is step 2 of 7 of Light or Dark. Here you set up the seeds and place one set in the light and one in the dark.

flow.do: 1. Ask whether the dark chapati will grow less, the same or more mould, and why. 2. Ask whether the dark seedlings will look like the light ones, and why. 3. Write the guesses down.
flow.say: A plant makes food from light. If a mould were a kind of plant, what should happen to the mould in the dark? What do you think will happen?
flow.kid: Guess what the mould will do in the dark. Guess what the seedlings will do. Say why. Write it down.

good: Mould grows in dark cupboards, so I think the dark will not stop them.
Plants need light, so the dark seedlings will not be healthy.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Many children expect everything to grow worse in the dark.
flow.context: This is step 3 of 7 of Light or Dark. This step is for guessing. You guess before anything has grown.

flow.do: 1. Lift the box. 2. Look at both pouches without opening them. 3. Look at both saucers. 4. Write what you see in the table. 5. Add one teaspoon of water to each seed pad and put the box back.
flow.say: It is day 3. What has changed on each chapati? What colour are the seedlings in each saucer?
flow.kid: Lift the box. Look through the pouches. Look at the seedlings. Write what you see. Add a teaspoon of water to each pad.
flow.parent: Mould may not show yet. Seeds sprout in both saucers, because a seed needs water and warmth to sprout, not light.
flow.context: This is step 4 of 7 of Light or Dark. Here you make the first check, on day 3.

flow.do: 1. Lift the box and look at all four again. 2. Write what you see in the table. 3. Add one teaspoon of water to each seed pad. 4. Put the box back.
flow.say: It is day 5. Is there mould now? Is there more on one chapati than on the other? How do the two lots of seedlings differ?
flow.kid: Look at all four again. Is there mould? How do the seedlings differ? Write it down. Add water to each pad.
flow.context: This is step 5 of 7 of Light or Dark. Here you make the second check, on day 5.

flow.do: 1. Judge how much of each chapati is covered with mould, looking through the pouch. 2. Measure the height of five seedlings from each saucer. 3. Write the colours and heights in the table. 4. Put the sealed pouches in the dustbin.
flow.say: It is day 7. How much of each chapati is covered? Measure five seedlings from each saucer and tell me their colour.
flow.kid: Judge the mould through the pouch. Measure five seedlings from each saucer. Write the colours and heights. Bin the sealed pouches.
flow.parent: Expect about the same mould in the light and in the dark. Expect the dark seedlings to be taller, thinner and pale yellow, with small leaves. If no mould has grown by day 7, keep the pouches three more days. A dry or cold room slows mould down.
flow.context: This is step 6 of 7 of Light or Dark. Here you make the last check, on day 7, and measure the seedlings.

flow.do: 1. Your child writes three sentences: what they thought, what they saw and why it happened. 2. Ask where the mould got food in the dark. 3. Ask where the dark seedlings got food to grow so tall. 4. Move the yellow seedlings into the light for two days.
flow.say: Write your claim, your evidence and your reason. The mould grew with no light at all. So where did their food come from?
flow.kid: Write what you thought. Write what you saw. Write why it happened. Where did the mould get food in the dark?

ask.q: The dark seedlings grew taller than the light ones. Does that show that plants do not need light?
good: No. They were using up the food stored in the seed.
They were yellow and thin. They grew tall to search for light, and they made no new food.

flow.parent: The mould's food was the chapati. The seedlings in the dark were spending the food packed in the seed, and making none. Kept in the dark, they would run out and die in about two weeks. In the light, the yellow seedlings turn green within a day or two.

check.q: A mould grew as well in the dark as in the light. What does that show about how a mould feeds?
options: A mould does not make food from light
A mould makes food faster in the dark
check.why: A mould does not make food from light. They digest the chapati and soak it up. 'Faster in the dark' still treats the mould as a food-maker. 'Needs no food' forgets the chapati, which the mould was eating.

flow.context: This is the last step of Light or Dark. Here you write what you found and explain where the mould and the seedlings got their food.

activities.title: The Two-Box Problem: can everything alive at home be a plant or an animal?
activities.context: In this activity you name ten living beings who share your home, and try to sort them all into two boxes, plants and animals. You find out who does not fit.

materials.item: a sheet of paper cut into 10 slips
a second sheet of paper and a pencil

activities.record: Draw the two boxes and write each being's name where you put them. Draw a ring round every being who did not fit either box.

setup.art: Ten paper slips on a table with names written on them, among them 'tulsi plant', 'ant', 'me', 'curd bacteria', 'yeast in bread' and 'mould on a lemon'.
setup.caption: 1. Write the names of ten living beings from your home on ten slips.

setup.art: A sheet of paper divided by a line into two halves headed Plants and Animals, with some slips placed in each half and four slips lying on the line between.
setup.caption: 2. Sort them into two boxes. Put the ones who do not fit on the line.

flow.do: 1. Write ten names on ten slips. 2. The first five are a potted plant, coriander leaves, an ant, a house gecko or a crow, and yourself. 3. Three more are the bacteria in curd, the yeast in bread and a mushroom. 4. The last two are the mould on old fruit and the green film in a flowerpot saucer. 5. Ask how many of the ten will fit into 'plants' or 'animals'.
flow.say: All ten of these are alive, or were alive when they came into our kitchen. How many of them are plants or animals? Guess a number.
flow.kid: Write ten living beings from your home on slips. Use the list. Guess how many are plants or animals.
flow.parent: Change the list to fit your home, but keep the curd bacteria, the yeast, the mushroom and the mould. If there is no mushroom in the house, write the slip anyway.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Two-Box Problem. Here you write ten living beings from your home on slips of paper.

flow.do: 1. Draw a line down a sheet of paper. 2. Head one half 'Plants' and the other 'Animals'. 3. Your child places each slip and gives a reason. 4. Slips that fit neither half go on the line.
flow.say: Put each slip in a box and tell me your rule. If a being fits neither box, put that slip on the line.
flow.kid: Draw two boxes: Plants and Animals. Put each slip in a box. Say your rule. Put the ones who do not fit on the line.

ask.q: What is your rule for 'plant'? Does the mushroom pass it?
good: A plant is green and makes food from light. The mushroom is not green.
A plant stays still. But that would make the mushroom a plant, and I am not sure.

flow.parent: Do not settle the hard slips. Usually the curd bacteria, the yeast, the mushroom and the mould end up on the line or cause an argument. The green film is mostly algae and cyanobacteria.
flow.context: This step of the Two-Box Problem sorts the ten slips into plants and animals.

flow.do: 1. Count the slips on the line. 2. Ask what you would need to find out about each one to place them. 3. Write the questions down and keep them.
flow.say: Some beings did not fit. What would we need to know about them? Let's write our questions and keep them.
flow.kid: Count the slips on the line. What would you need to know about them? Write your questions.
flow.think: People used only these two boxes for two thousand years. What do you think made them add more?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Two-Box Problem. Here you count who did not fit, and write down what you would need to find out.

activities.title: Four Maps of Life: sort the same twelve beings in 1735, 1866, 1969 and today
activities.context: In this activity you sort the same twelve living beings four times, the way scientists did in four different years. You count how often each being had to move, and find out which beings caused the redrawing.

materials.item: a sheet of paper cut into 12 slips
sheets of paper for the four maps
a pencil

activities.record: Make a table with twelve rows, one for each being, and four columns, one for each year. Write the group each being was in. In a last column, count how many times that being changed group.

setup.art: Twelve paper slips with the names of living beings, among them 'human', 'moss', 'mushroom', 'amoeba', 'brown seaweed' and 'methane-maker'.
setup.caption: 1. Write twelve beings on twelve slips.

setup.art: Four sheets of paper in a row headed 1735, 1866, 1969 and Today, divided into two, three, five and three boxes.
setup.caption: 2. Draw four maps: two groups, three groups, five groups and three domains.

setup.art: A child moving the slip 'mushroom' from a box marked Plants on one sheet to a box marked Fungi on the next sheet.
setup.caption: 3. Sort all twelve on each map in turn. Count who moves.

flow.do: 1. Write these on 12 slips: human, gecko, sponge, coconut palm, moss, mushroom, yeast, amoeba, Euglena, brown seaweed, curd bacterium, methane-maker. 2. Head the first sheet '1735' and divide it into Plants and Animals. 3. Your child sorts the slips and writes the result in the table.
flow.say: It is 1735. There are two kingdoms, plants and animals. Nobody has a microscope good enough to see inside a cell. Where does each being go?
flow.kid: Write the twelve beings on slips. Draw the 1735 map: Plants and Animals. Sort the slips. Write where each one went.
flow.parent: Under the two kingdoms, the mushroom, yeast, seaweed, moss and palm were plants. The amoeba, once people had seen one, was called an animal. Bacteria were put with the plants. Euglena was claimed by both sides. The sponge was argued over, and settled as an animal in the 1800s.
flow.context: This is the first step of Four Maps of Life. Here you sort twelve living beings the way people did in 1735.

flow.do: 1. Head the second sheet '1866'. 2. Divide it into Plants, Animals and Protists. 3. Explain that Protists were the tiny beings who were neither plant nor animal. 4. Your child sorts again and writes the result.
flow.say: It is 1866. Microscopes are good, and Ernst Haeckel adds a third kingdom for tiny beings who are neither plant nor animal. Who moves?
flow.kid: Draw the 1866 map: Plants, Animals and Protists. Sort the slips again. Write who moved.
flow.parent: The amoeba, Euglena and both microbes move to Protists. Haeckel counted bacteria among the protists. The mushroom and the yeast stayed with the plants in most books.
flow.context: This step of Four Maps of Life sorts the twelve beings the way Ernst Haeckel did in 1866.

flow.do: 1. Head the third sheet '1969'. 2. Divide it into five: Monera, Protists, Fungi, Plants and Animals. 3. Explain that Monera means every cell with no nucleus. 4. Your child sorts again and writes the result.
flow.say: It is 1969. The electron microscope has shown the nucleus clearly, and Robert Whittaker has looked at how each being feeds. Who moves now?
flow.kid: Draw the 1969 map with five kingdoms. Sort the slips again. Write who moved.
flow.parent: The curd bacterium and the methane-maker go to Monera. The mushroom and the yeast go to Fungi. The amoeba and Euglena stay in Protists. Whittaker left the brown seaweed in Plants.
flow.context: This step of Four Maps of Life sorts the twelve beings into Robert Whittaker's five kingdoms of 1969.

flow.do: 1. Head the fourth sheet 'Today'. 2. Divide it into Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya. 3. Inside Eukarya, draw rings for Animals, Fungi, Plants and 'other branches'. 4. Your child sorts again and writes the result.
flow.say: Today scientists can read genes. Carl Woese found that the methane-makers are not bacteria at all. Where does everyone go now?
flow.kid: Draw today's map: Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya. Add rings inside Eukarya. Sort the slips again. Write who moved.
flow.parent: The curd bacterium goes to Bacteria and the methane-maker to Archaea. All ten others go to Eukarya. The amoeba, Euglena and the brown seaweed go in 'other branches', each on a different branch.
flow.context: This step of Four Maps of Life sorts the twelve beings into the three domains used today.

flow.do: 1. Your child counts how many times each being changed group. 2. Ask who never moved and who moved most. 3. Ask what new tool came before each new map.
flow.say: Who never moved in three hundred years? Who moved nearly every time? What was different about the ones who moved?
flow.kid: Count each being's moves. Who never moved? Who moved most? What do the movers share?

ask.q: Why did the human, the gecko, the palm and the moss never move?
good: People could always see them clearly.
The beings who moved were small or hard to see inside, so each new tool showed something new.

flow.think: What tool might redraw the map next?
flow.context: This is the last step of Four Maps of Life. Here you count the moves and look for what the moving beings have in common.

activities.title: Six Questions: build a key for the big groups of life
activities.context: In this activity you write a branching key of yes-or-no questions that sorts any living being into one of the big groups. Then you test your key on the cards from the game Which Kingdom?, and try to break it with hard cases.

materials.item: the 24 being cards from the game Which Kingdom?
a large sheet of paper and a pencil

activities.record: Keep the finished key. Beside it, list any being that your key sorted wrongly, and the question you changed to mend it.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a branching diagram of boxes joined by lines marked yes and no, the top box reading 'Do the cells have a nucleus?'.
setup.caption: 1. Write a first question. Draw a 'yes' line and a 'no' line from it.

setup.art: A child's finger following the lines of a hand-drawn key while the other hand holds a card showing a mushroom.
setup.caption: 2. Take a card. Follow your key to the end. Turn the card to check.

setup.art: The same key with one question crossed out and rewritten, and a card showing a brown seaweed lying beside it.
setup.caption: 3. When a card breaks the key, change a question and test again.

flow.do: 1. Write at the top of the sheet: 'Do the cells have a nucleus?' 2. Draw a 'no' line and a 'yes' line. 3. Your child adds questions until every line ends at one group. 4. The groups are Bacteria, Archaea, Protists, Fungi, Plants and Animals.
flow.say: A key is a chain of yes-or-no questions. Each answer sends you down one line. What question would you ask next on the 'yes' side?
flow.kid: Start with: do the cells have a nucleus? Draw a yes line and a no line. Add questions until each line ends at one group.
flow.parent: One key that works: no nucleus, then 'Do they make methane, or have the unusual membrane fats?' gives Archaea or Bacteria. With a nucleus: 'Many cells, no cell walls, food taken inside?' gives Animals. 'Chitin walls, soaks up food?' gives Fungi. 'Cellulose walls and green chloroplasts?' gives Plants. Everyone else is a Protist. Let your child find their own questions first.
flow.context: This is the first step of Six Questions. Here you write a key of yes-or-no questions for the big groups of life.

flow.do: 1. Shuffle the being cards. 2. Your child takes eight cards, one at a time. 3. For each, they follow the key using only the clues, then turn the card. 4. They mark each result right or wrong.
flow.say: Now test the key. Use only the clues on the card. Does your key send this being to the right group?
flow.kid: Take eight cards. Follow your key for each one. Turn the card to check. Mark right or wrong.

ask.q: Your key says 'no nucleus' first. Why is that a good first question?
good: It splits life at the biggest difference in how cells are built.
It needs no other question first.

flow.context: This step of Six Questions tests your key on eight cards from the game Which Kingdom?.

flow.do: 1. Find the cards for Euglena, the brown seaweed and the lichen. 2. Your child runs each through the key. 3. Where the key gives a wrong answer, they change one question and test again.
flow.say: Here are three hard cases. Does your key still work? If it breaks, which question needs to change?
flow.kid: Try Euglena, the brown seaweed and the lichen. Does your key break? Change one question. Test again.
flow.parent: A question such as 'Do they photosynthesise?' sends Euglena and the seaweed to Plants. No key of this kind can place the lichen, who is two beings. It is fine to end with 'this key cannot sort a lichen'. Scientists settle hard cases by reading genes.
flow.think: A key sorts by features you can check. A family tree sorts by ancestors. When might the two disagree?
flow.context: This is the last step of Six Questions. Here you test the key on three hard cases and mend it.

activities.title: The Weight of Life: a paper strip for every big group
activities.context: In this activity you make a paper strip 55 centimetres long that stands for the weight of all life on Earth. You mark off a length for each big group, to see which groups hold most of the living material.

materials.item: sheets of plain paper
scissors and sticky tape or glue
a ruler marked in millimetres
colour pencils or sketch pens in six colours

activities.record: Keep the strip. Write on each part the name of the group and the number of billion tonnes. On the back, write your first guess of the order, and how it compares.

setup.art: Two long strips of paper being taped end to end, with a ruler beside them showing a total length of 55 centimetres.
setup.caption: 1. Tape strips together to make one strip 55 centimetres long.

setup.art: A long paper strip with a very long green part, a shorter blue part and several very narrow coloured bands at the end, each labelled.
setup.caption: 2. Mark off a length for each group. One millimetre stands for one billion tonnes of carbon.

setup.art: A close view of the last few millimetres of the strip, with a sharp pencil making the thinnest possible line labelled 'all humans'.
setup.caption: 3. Find the 2 millimetres for all animals. Humans are thinner than one pencil line.

flow.do: 1. Write the six groups on paper: plants, animals, fungi, bacteria, archaea, protists. 2. Ask your child to put them in order, from the heaviest in total to the lightest. 3. Ask for the reason. 4. Write the guess down.
flow.say: Suppose we could weigh all the plants on Earth together, then all the animals, and so on. Which group is heaviest? Which is lightest? Why?
flow.kid: Put the six groups in order, heaviest first. Say why. Write your guess.
flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children put animals near the top.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Weight of Life. This step is for guessing which big groups of life weigh the most.

flow.do: 1. Cut strips 3 centimetres wide and tape them into one strip 55 centimetres long. 2. From one end, mark 450 millimetres for plants. 3. Then mark 70 for bacteria, 12 for fungi, 7 for archaea, 4 for protists and 2 for animals. 4. Colour and label each part. 5. Leave the last 5 millimetres blank.
flow.say: One millimetre stands for one billion tonnes of carbon in living beings. Plants get 450 millimetres. Measure each group in turn.
flow.kid: Make a strip 55 cm long. Mark 450 mm for plants. Then 70, 12, 7, 4 and 2. Colour and label each part.
flow.parent: The figures come from a study of 2018 and are rounded estimates, so they add up to 545 and not 550. The blank 5 millimetres stand for that rounding. The figures for microbes are the least certain.
flow.context: This step of the Weight of Life marks off a length of the paper strip for each big group.

flow.do: 1. Find the 2 millimetres for animals. 2. Explain that all humans together are 0.06 of a millimetre. 3. Your child draws the thinnest line they can inside the animal part.
flow.say: All eight billion humans together are six hundredths of a millimetre on this strip. Draw the thinnest line you can. It is still too thick.
flow.kid: Find the 2 mm for animals. Draw the thinnest line you can inside it. All humans are thinner than that.

ask.q: Fungi weigh six times as much as all animals. Why do we hardly notice them?
good: Most of a fungus is fine threads hidden in soil and wood.
We only see the mushrooms, which are a small part.

flow.context: This step of the Weight of Life finds the share of animals and of humans on the strip.

flow.do: 1. Compare the strip with the first guess. 2. Ask which result was the biggest surprise. 3. Ask why plants weigh so much.
flow.say: How close was your guess? Trees hold most of the weight of life. What are trees mostly made of, that lets them be so heavy?
flow.kid: Compare the strip with your guess. What surprised you most? Why do plants weigh so much?
flow.parent: Most plant weight is wood: the cellulose walls of cells in tree trunks, much of it no longer living. By variety, microbes have the most branches on the tree of life. By weight, plants are far ahead. Animals are small on both counts.
flow.think: Plants have the most weight. Microbes have the most kinds. Which is the better way to measure a group's share of life?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Weight of Life. Here you compare the finished strip with your first guess.

activities.title: Tree or Web? Draw the places where branches join
activities.context: In this activity you draw the tree of life with three domains, and then add the two great joins: the bacteria who became mitochondria and the bacteria who became chloroplasts. You trace how many lines of ancestors lead to your own cells, and to a leaf.

materials.item: a large sheet of paper
a pencil, and a red and a green colour pencil

activities.record: Keep the drawing. Under it, write how many lines of ancestors lead back from a curd bacterium, from one of your own cells and from a neem leaf cell.

setup.art: A pencil drawing of a tree with one root splitting into a branch labelled Bacteria and a second branch that splits again into Archaea and Eukarya, with twigs for animals, fungi and plants.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the tree: Bacteria on one side, Archaea and Eukarya on the other.

setup.art: The same tree with a red line crossing from the Bacteria branch to the base of the Eukarya branch, and a green line crossing from a twig marked cyanobacteria to the plant twig.
setup.caption: 2. Add a red join for mitochondria and a green join for chloroplasts.

setup.art: A child's finger tracing back from the tip of the plant twig along three different coloured paths towards the root.
setup.caption: 3. Trace back from a leaf cell. Count the paths.

flow.do: 1. Draw one line up from the bottom of the page and split it in two. 2. Label the left branch Bacteria and give it a twig marked 'cyanobacteria'. 3. Split the right branch into Archaea and Eukarya. 4. On Eukarya, draw twigs for animals, fungi, plants and two protists.
flow.say: This is the tree with three domains. Every fork is an ancestor. On a tree like this, can two branches ever join again?
flow.kid: Draw a line and split it in two. Left is Bacteria. Split the right into Archaea and Eukarya. Add twigs for animals, fungi and plants.
flow.parent: Put the animal twig and the fungus twig on one small fork, to show that they are nearest relatives.
flow.context: This is the first step of Tree or Web? Here you draw the tree of life with three domains.

flow.do: 1. With red, draw a line from the middle of the Bacteria branch across to the base of the Eukarya branch. 2. Label it 'became mitochondria'. 3. With green, draw a line from the cyanobacteria twig across to the base of the plant twig. 4. Label it 'became chloroplasts'.
flow.say: About two billion years ago, a bacterium began living inside another cell and stayed. Later, a cyanobacterium did the same in the ancestor of plants.
flow.kid: Draw a red line from Bacteria to the base of Eukarya. Draw a green line from cyanobacteria to the plants. Label both.
flow.context: This step of Tree or Web? adds the two great joins: mitochondria and chloroplasts.

flow.do: 1. Your child puts a finger on a curd bacterium on the Bacteria branch and traces back to the root. 2. They do the same from the animal twig, following every line that leads in. 3. They do the same from the plant twig. 4. They count the paths each time.
flow.say: Trace back from each tip to the root. Follow the coloured lines too. How many different paths lead back from each one?
flow.kid: Trace back from the bacterium. Trace back from the animal twig. Trace back from the plant twig. Count the paths each time.

ask.q: How many paths lead back from one of your cells? How many from a leaf cell?
good: Two from mine: the cell itself and the mitochondria.
Three from a leaf cell: the cell, the mitochondria and the chloroplasts.

check.q: A neem leaf cell has a nucleus, mitochondria and chloroplasts. How many lines of ancestors meet in that cell?
check.why: Three: the cell with the nucleus, the bacteria who became mitochondria and the cyanobacteria who became chloroplasts. 'One' treats the cell as a single line of descent. 'Two' leaves out the chloroplasts, which animal cells do not have.

flow.context: This step of Tree or Web? traces the lines of ancestors back from a bacterium, an animal cell and a plant cell.

flow.do: 1. Ask whether the drawing is still a tree. 2. Ask what else could cross between branches. 3. Your child adds three thin dotted lines between microbe branches for single genes passed sideways.
flow.say: Is this still a tree? Bacteria also pass single genes to their neighbours. Add a few thin dotted lines for those.
flow.kid: Is it still a tree? Add three thin dotted lines between the microbe branches. They stand for genes passed sideways.
flow.think: If you had to choose one word for this drawing, would it be 'tree', 'web' or something else?
flow.context: This is the last step of Tree or Web? Here you add genes passed sideways and decide what to call the drawing.

projects.title: A Census of Our Home: how many of the big groups of life live with us?
projects.context: In this three-day project you look for members of every big group of life in and around your home. For each one you write how you know they are there: you saw them, you saw what they did, or you read about them.

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil
a hand lens (useful, not needed)
chart paper, or two sheets of paper taped together
colour pencils

projects.safety: Do not touch mould, wild mushrooms or animal droppings. Look, and wash your hands with soap afterwards. A grown-up comes along for the search outside the home.

schedule.what: Guess how many of the six groups live in your home. Search the kitchen and the rooms, and list every being with your evidence.
Search the balcony, the stairs and the street with a grown-up. Look at walls, tree trunks, flowerpots and puddles.
Make a poster with six columns. Count the entries, and write what the count shows and what it hides.

projects.record: Keep a list with three columns: the being, the group, and your evidence ('I saw them', 'I saw what they did' or 'I read about them'). On day 3, turn the list into a poster with six columns and write four sentences about what you found.

setup.art: A child with a notebook looking into a kitchen shelf holding a bowl of curd, a loaf of bread, a packet of mushrooms and a bunch of coriander.
setup.caption: 1. Search the home. List every living being and how you know they are there.

setup.art: A child with a hand lens looking closely at a grey-green lichen and a patch of moss on a compound wall, with a grown-up beside them.
setup.caption: 2. Search outside with a grown-up. Look at walls, tree trunks and flowerpots.

setup.art: A hand-drawn poster with six columns headed Bacteria, Archaea, Protists, Fungi, Plants and Animals, with small drawings and three kinds of tick marks.
setup.caption: 3. Make a poster with six columns and mark the kind of evidence for each being.

flow.do: 1. Your child guesses how many of the six groups live in the home, and why. 2. Search the kitchen and the rooms together. 3. For each being, your child writes the name, the group and the evidence. 4. Remind them of the beings they cannot see.
flow.say: Six big groups: bacteria, archaea, protists, fungi, plants and animals. How many live in our home? For each one we find, how do we know?
flow.kid: Guess how many groups live in your home. Search the kitchen and rooms. Write each being, the group and your evidence.
flow.parent: Animals and plants are easy. For fungi, look for mushrooms, bread or batter raised by yeast, and mould on old fruit. Curd is evidence of bacteria: you see what they did. So is the soft coat on teeth in the morning. Archaea cannot be seen at home. Many people have methane-making archaea in their gut, so 'I read about them' is honest evidence.
flow.context: This is day 1 of A Census of Our Home. Here you search inside the home and list every living being you find evidence for.

flow.do: 1. Go out together to the balcony, the stairs and the street. 2. Look closely at damp walls, tree trunks, flowerpot saucers and puddles. 3. Your child adds each new being to the list, with the group and the evidence. 4. Wash hands with soap when you come in.
flow.say: Look for the small and the flat: green films, grey crusts on tree trunks, moss, mushrooms after rain. Which group could each one be?
flow.kid: Go outside with a grown-up. Look at walls, tree trunks and flowerpots. Add each new being to your list. Wash your hands after.

ask.q: You found a green film in a flowerpot saucer. How could you find out which group they belong to?
good: Look under a microscope to see if the cells have a nucleus.
Green could mean algae or cyanobacteria, so colour alone is not enough.

flow.parent: A grey-green crust on a trunk or a wall is usually a lichen, a fungus and an alga together. Green slime is usually algae, who are protists or plants in the wide sense, or cyanobacteria. It is fine to write 'protist or bacteria: not sure'.
flow.context: This is day 2 of A Census of Our Home. Here you search outside the home with a grown-up.

flow.do: 1. Your child rules six columns on the chart paper and heads them with the six groups. 2. They enter every being, with a mark for the kind of evidence. 3. They count the entries in each column. 4. They write four sentences about what the count shows and what it hides.
flow.say: Which column is longest? Is that because that group has the most kinds, or because they are the easiest for us to see?
flow.kid: Rule six columns. Enter every being. Mark your evidence. Count each column. Write four sentences about what you found.

ask.q: Your animal column is probably the longest. Scientists say microbes have the most kinds. Why do the two counts differ?
good: We list what we can see, and microbes are too small to see.
One spoon of soil holds more kinds of bacteria than all the animals on our list.

flow.parent: A strong report notices that the method decides the result. A census made by eye finds big beings. A census made by reading genes from soil finds mostly microbes.
flow.context: This is day 3 of A Census of Our Home. Here you make the poster, count the entries and write what you found.

challenges.title: A Chart That Survives a New Discovery
challenges.context: This is a design challenge on paper. The chart of the big groups of life has been redrawn many times, because new beings kept turning up who did not fit. Here you design a chart that can take in a new discovery without being drawn all over again.
challenges.problem: Design a wall chart of the big groups of life. It must be possible to add a newly discovered being, or move a group, by changing only one line or one label. Then test your chart with three discoveries.
constraints: The chart fits on one sheet of chart paper.
It shows bacteria, archaea, protists, fungi, plants and animals, and who is nearest to whom.
Each of the three test discoveries must be added by changing no more than one line or one label.
A label for leftovers, such as 'protists', must look different from a real branch.
materials: a sheet of chart paper, or two sheets of paper taped together
small slips of paper and sticky tape, or sticky notes
thread or wool, if you have it
general: Draw a table with one box for each group. This is the usual school chart.
Draw a branching tree in ink, with the group names written at the tips.
creative: Draw the tree in pencil and write the group names on loose slips, so that a name can be moved without redrawing a branch.
Show each named group as a loop of thread laid round the twigs it covers. To change a group, move the loop.
Leave a corner of the chart headed 'not yet placed', as museums do for beings whose relatives are still unknown.
Draw the tree as a circle with the root in the middle, so that there is room to add twigs all the way round.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own chart. Build it and test it with the three discoveries. How many lines or labels did each one make you change? What would you tell a scientist who wants to add a seventh group?

setup.art: A neat table of six boxes, each holding the name of one big group of life, drawn on chart paper.
setup.caption: 1. Start with the usual chart: one box for each group.

setup.art: Three small paper slips reading 'a new cell with a nucleus who fits no kingdom', 'archaea who are nearer to us than to other archaea' and 'a giant virus'.
setup.caption: 2. Write the three discoveries on slips. Try to add each one.

setup.art: A pencil-drawn tree of life on chart paper with group names on movable paper slips and a loop of wool laid round three twigs.
setup.caption: 3. Redesign the chart so that each discovery needs only one change.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws the usual chart: six boxes, one for each group. 2. Write the three discoveries on three slips. 3. Your child tries to add the first one to the box chart.
flow.say: Here is the first discovery: a new cell with a nucleus, who is not an animal, a plant, a fungus or like any known protist. Where do they go?
flow.kid: Draw six boxes, one for each group. Read the first discovery slip. Try to add them to your chart.
flow.parent: The three slips are: 'a new cell with a nucleus who fits no kingdom', 'archaea who are nearer relatives of us than of other archaea', and 'a giant virus with a thousand genes'. All three are real discoveries of the last twenty-five years.
flow.context: This is the first step of A Chart That Survives a New Discovery. Here you draw the usual box chart and try to add a new being to it.

flow.do: 1. Your child tries the second and third slips on the box chart. 2. Ask what had to be redrawn each time. 3. Look together at the usual ideas and the creative ideas. 4. Your child sketches a new design.
flow.say: What broke when you added the second discovery? What kind of chart would have bent and not broken?
flow.kid: Try the other two slips. What had to be redrawn? Look at the ideas. Sketch a better chart.

ask.q: Why does a box chart break more easily than a tree?
good: Boxes show no links between groups, so a being who sits between two groups has no place.
On a tree you can add a twig. In a table you must add or split a whole box.

flow.context: This step of A Chart That Survives a New Discovery tests the box chart with two more discoveries and plans a better design.

flow.do: 1. Your child builds the new chart. 2. They add all three discoveries, counting the changes each one needs. 3. They mark the 'protists' label so that it looks different from a real branch.
flow.say: Add the three discoveries to your new chart. Count the changes. Did any one of them need more than a single line or label?
flow.kid: Build your new chart. Add the three discoveries. Count the changes each one needs. Make 'protists' look different from a branch.
flow.parent: There is no perfect answer. Real scientists disagree about how to draw this. A good design makes it easy to see what is known, what is a label of convenience and what is still open.
flow.context: This is the last step of A Chart That Survives a New Discovery. Here you build your new chart and test it with all three discoveries.

challenges.title: A Fair Tree for the Wall
challenges.context: This is a design challenge on paper. Most posters of life give nearly all the space to animals. Here you design a poster of the tree of life that shares the space fairly, and you must decide what 'fair' means.
challenges.problem: Design a poster of the tree of life on one sheet. Choose one rule for how much space each big group gets, and write the rule on the poster in one sentence.
constraints: The poster shows three domains, and animals, fungi and plants inside one of them.
The space each group gets follows your one rule, with no exceptions.
A six-year-old must be able to find the human on it.
The rule is written on the poster in one sentence.
materials: a pencil, a ruler and colour pencils
the paper strip from the Weight of Life, if you made it
general: Give every group the same space.
Give each group space by weight, using the Weight of Life figures. Plants then take four fifths of the poster.
creative: Give space by age: how long ago each branch split off. Bacteria and archaea then get long branches, and animals a short one.
Give space by the number of named kinds. Animals then fill most of the poster, because people name what they can see.
Make two small trees side by side with two different rules, so that the reader sees how the rule changes the picture.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own fair tree. Draw it and show it to someone. Ask them which group looks most important. Is that what your rule meant to say? What would a bacterium choose as the rule?

setup.art: A typical poster of life crowded with large drawings of a tiger, an elephant and a peacock, with one tiny corner labelled 'microbes'.
setup.caption: 1. Look at a usual poster of life. Who gets the space?

setup.art: A child writing one sentence at the top of a sheet of chart paper, with a ruler and a pencil-drawn tree of life below it.
setup.caption: 2. Choose one rule for sharing the space. Write it in one sentence.
