flow.do: 1. Ask your child to picture a poster called 'Life on Earth'. 2. Ask which beings fill it. 3. Read the usual rules and the creative rules together. 4. Your child chooses one rule and says why it is fair.
flow.say: A usual poster of life is nearly all animals. Is that fair? Choose one rule for sharing the space, and tell me why it is fair.
flow.kid: Picture a poster of life. Who fills it? Choose one rule for sharing the space. Say why it is fair.
flow.context: This is the first step of A Fair Tree for the Wall. Here you choose the rule that decides how much space each group gets.

flow.do: 1. Your child writes the rule at the top of the chart paper. 2. They work out the share for each group. 3. They draw the tree with three domains, giving each group their share. 4. They mark the human.
flow.say: Work out each group's share by your rule first. Then draw. Keep to the rule, even where the result looks odd.
flow.kid: Write your rule at the top. Work out each group's share. Draw the tree. Mark the human.
flow.parent: For the weight rule, the figures are plants 450, bacteria 70, fungi 12, archaea 7, protists 4 and animals 2. For the age rule, bacteria and archaea split more than 3.5 billion years ago, cells with a nucleus appeared about 2 billion years ago, and animals about 600 million years ago. These dates are rough and still argued over.
flow.context: This step of A Fair Tree for the Wall draws the tree of life by the rule you chose.

flow.do: 1. Your child shows the poster to someone who has not seen it. 2. That person finds the human and says which group looks most important. 3. Your child explains the rule. 4. Together, name one thing the rule hides.
flow.say: Ask your viewer to find the human. Ask which group looks most important. Is that what your rule meant to show?
flow.kid: Show your poster to someone. Can they find the human? Which group looks biggest to them? Explain your rule.

ask.q: Every rule made some group look small. Is there any rule that is fair to everyone?
good: No. Each rule measures one thing, such as weight, age or number of kinds.
A fair poster says which rule it used, so the reader is not misled.

flow.context: This is the last step of A Fair Tree for the Wall. Here you test the poster on another person and look at what your rule hides.

items.p: Which part does a mushroom cell have that a bacterium does not?
items.why: A mushroom is a eukaryote, so each cell has a nucleus. Every cell of every kind has a membrane, genes and ribosomes, so those three cannot tell the two apart.

items.p: True or false: a mushroom makes food from sunlight.
items.why: False. A mushroom has no chlorophyll and cannot photosynthesise. A mushroom digests food such as dead wood or straw. Thinking 'true' usually comes from seeing mushrooms as plants.

items.p: A fungus feeds by digesting food ____ their body and then soaking it up.
items.why: A fungus lets digesting juices out onto the food and soaks up the result. An animal takes food inside the body first.

items.p: Match each group to one thing that marks it.
items.why: Each mark is a feature of how the cells are built or how the being feeds. A strong answer could add an example of each group.

items.p: Sort these: do their cells have a nucleus or not?
items.why: Bacteria and archaea have no nucleus. Yeast, amoebae and mosses are eukaryotes. Size does not decide it: a yeast is a single cell and still has a nucleus.

items.p: Which group is a label for 'everyone left over', and not one family?
items.why: Protists are all the eukaryotes who are not animals, plants or fungi. They sit on many separate branches. Fungi, animals and plants are each one whole branch.

items.p: In the Two-Box Problem, which beings from your home fitted neither 'plants' nor 'animals'? Why not?
items.a: Answers vary. Usually the curd bacteria, the yeast, the mushroom and the mould. They do not photosynthesise like plants, and they do not move about and swallow food like animals.
items.why: A strong answer names the beings and gives the feature that failed each box, such as 'not green, so not a plant' and 'no mouth, so not an animal'.

items.p: Put these ways of sorting life in order, from the earliest to the latest.
a: A third kingdom is added for protists
Five kingdoms, with fungi on their own
Three domains, with archaea apart from bacteria
items.why: Each step followed a new tool. Better light microscopes showed the protists. The electron microscope and studies of feeding gave five kingdoms. Gene reading gave three domains.
items: Five kingdoms, with fungi on their own
Three domains, with archaea apart from bacteria
A third kingdom is added for protists

items.p: True or false: archaea are a kind of bacteria.
items.why: False. Both have cells with no nucleus, but their genes and membranes differ deeply. Archaea are closer relatives of us than of bacteria.

items.p: Scientists compare the same gene in two beings. What do fewer differing letters mean?
opts: They shared an ancestor more recently
They live in the same place
items.why: Changes build up with time, so few differences mean little time since the two were one family. Looks, place and size can match in beings who are not close relatives.

items.p: Draw a mushroom, and the part of the fungus that is hidden under the ground. Label the hyphae.
items.a: A mushroom above the ground, joined to a wide web of fine threads spreading through the soil. The threads are labelled hyphae.
items.why: The mushroom is only the part that makes spores. Most of the fungus is the web of hyphae, which does the feeding.
items.art: A blank strip of ground seen from the side, with space above and below the soil line.

items.p: Three of these are fungi. Which one is not?
items.why: Moss is a plant, with chloroplasts and cellulose walls. Yeast, bread mould and oyster mushrooms all feed by soaking up food and have chitin in their walls.

items.p: The gas in a gobar gas plant is made by tiny beings called ____.
items.why: Every known being who makes methane is an archaeon. They live where there is no oxygen, as inside the tank.

items.p: In the Hidden Tree Test, bodies and letters disagreed about the sisters. Which was right? How do you know?
items.a: The letters were right. The sisters differed in only 4 letters and the others in 8, and the hidden slips showed the same pairs. The bodies were not copied from the parent, so they did not show the family.
items.why: A strong answer uses the numbers as evidence and says that only the message was passed down by copying.

items.p: Here are two views about where mushrooms belong.

views.says: Mushrooms belong with the vegetables. We buy them, cut them and cook them in the same way.
Mushrooms belong nearer to the animals. Their genes and their cells say so.

items.ask: Which sorting would you use in a kitchen, and which in a science book? Give a reason for each.
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer says that each sorting is right for its job. The cook's sorting helps with cooking. The biologist's sorting tells you about cells, feeding and relatives.
items.why: There are many useful ways to sort. Only the sorting by relatives has an answer that does not depend on what the sorter wants.

items.p: A being is one cell with a nucleus and no cell wall, and wraps round food. Which group?
items.why: A nucleus rules out bacteria. No cell wall and wrapping round food rule out fungi and plants. One cell rules out animals. What is left is a protist, such as an amoeba.

items.p: Iodine turns a cut potato blue-black, but not a slice of mushroom. What does this tell you about fungi?
items.a: Iodine shows starch. Potato cells store starch, as plants do. A mushroom has none, because fungi store their spare food as glycogen, as animals do.
items.why: A strong answer links the test to stored food, and says that in this feature fungi are like animals and unlike plants.

items.p: Sort these beings into the scientists' groups.
items.why: Sponges and corals stay in one place, but they are animals. Brown seaweeds and diatoms photosynthesise, but they are on a protist branch, not the plant branch.

items.p: True or false: 'prokaryote' is the name of one family of living beings.
items.why: False. 'Prokaryote' describes a cell with no nucleus. Two very different groups have such cells, the bacteria and the archaea.

items.p: Why did Carl Woese compare a gene for part of the ribosome?
items.why: To compare all life, you need a gene that all life has. Every cell has ribosomes. The gene also changes slowly, so very old splits can still be read.

items.p: A group made of one ancestor and all of their descendants is called a ____.
items.why: A clade is one whole branch of the tree. Fungi are a clade. Protists are not, because the group leaves some descendants out.

items.p: Match each piece of evidence to what it shows.
items.why: Each conclusion in this unit rests on something that was measured or seen. A strong answer could say who would be surprised by each piece of evidence.
pairs: Mould grows well in the dark
fungi do not make food from light
Fungus walls are made of chitin
Methane-makers' ribosome gene is unlike bacteria's
Every cell uses the same DNA code

items.p: P differs from Q in 2 letters, R in 6 and S in 10. Order P's relatives, closest first.
items.why: Fewer differing letters mean a more recent shared ancestor. So Q is closest, then R, then S.

items.p: In Light or Dark, the mould grew with no light. Where did the mould's food come from?
items.a: From the chapati. The mould let out juices that digested the chapati, and soaked up the digested food.
items.why: A strong answer names the chapati as the food and says that the mould did not make food, but took it in from outside.

items.p: On both the two-domain tree and the three-domain tree, who is an archaeon's closer relative?
items.why: The two trees disagree about whether our branch is beside the archaea or inside them. Both put archaea nearer to us than to bacteria.

items.p: On a tree with three main branches, label Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya. Mark where animals, fungi and plants go.
a: Bacteria: the branch that splits off first
Archaea and Eukarya: the two branches that share a fork
Animals, fungi and plants: three twigs on the Eukarya branch, with animals and fungi sharing a fork
items.why: Archaea and Eukarya share a more recent ancestor with each other than with Bacteria. Animals, fungi and plants are all inside Eukarya.
items.art: An unlabelled tree with one root, a first fork into two, and one of those branches forking again, with several small twigs at the end of one branch.

items.p: Three of these are clades, whole branches of the tree. Which one is not?
items.why: Protists are what is left of the eukaryotes when animals, plants and fungi are taken out. A branch with parts taken out is not a clade.

items.p: True or false: by weight, animals are the biggest group of living beings.
items.why: False. Plants hold about 450 of the 550 billion tonnes of carbon in living beings. All animals together hold about 2.

items.p: A cyanobacterium photosynthesises. Give two reasons why scientists do not call them a plant.
items.a: Their cell has no nucleus, and every plant cell has one. Their genes place them among the bacteria. Plants are a branch of eukaryotes whose chloroplasts came from cyanobacteria.
items.why: A strong answer uses the build of the cell and the family tree, not just 'they are too small'.

items.p: Draw a tree of life. Add one line showing bacteria joining the eukaryote branch. Label what those bacteria became.
items.a: A tree with Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya, and a line crossing from the Bacteria branch to the base of the Eukarya branch, labelled 'mitochondria'.
items.why: The line shows that the history of life has joins as well as splits. The bacteria who moved in became the mitochondria of every eukaryote cell.
items.art: A blank sheet with a small root drawn at the bottom.

items.p: One book says there are five kingdoms. Another says three domains. Can both be right? Explain.
items.a: Yes, in part. Both can describe the same tree, and differ in where they draw the lines. But the five kingdoms put bacteria and archaea together in one group, and genes show that this group is not one branch.
items.why: A strong answer separates the tree, which is found by evidence, from the lines drawn on it, which are chosen. It also names what the five kingdoms get wrong.

items.p: Why do very old splits in the tree of life give scientists the most trouble?
opts: The same letter can change twice
items.why: Over billions of years the same place in a gene can change more than once, and a later change hides an earlier one. The count of differences then says less about time.

items.p: Here are two views about our place on the tree of life.

views.says: Cells with a nucleus are so different in build that they are a trunk of their own, beside the archaea.
Our kind of cell began inside the archaea. So we are one branch of the archaea.

items.ask: Which view do you find stronger? What new evidence could change your mind?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a view, gives a reason, and names evidence that would count against it, such as more archaea grown in a laboratory or trees built from more genes.
items.why: Scientists have not settled this. What matters is to say what evidence each view rests on, and what would change it.

items.p: True or false: evidence can settle how many kingdoms there are.
items.why: False. Evidence can settle who is related to whom. How big a branch must be to be called a kingdom is a choice that people make.

items.p: Some people call bacteria 'lower' forms of life. What does the tree of life say about that?
items.a: Every being alive today is at the tip of a twig, and all have been changing for the same length of time since the first cells. The tree has no top and no bottom. Bacteria are not earlier or lower. They are a different branch.
items.why: A strong answer says that all living beings are equally modern, and that 'lower' is not a measurement of anything.

items.p: Sort these: does the question have a true answer, or is it a choice people make?
items.why: Questions about ancestors and about what a cell contains can be answered by evidence. Questions about what to call a group, or how many groups to have, are choices.
items: Are fungi nearer to animals or to plants?
How many kingdoms should there be?
Should protists be called a kingdom?
Is this branch big enough to be a domain?

items.p: Infections caused by fungi are often harder to treat than those caused by bacteria. Why?
opts: Fungus cells are much like ours
Fungi are too small to reach
Fungi are a kind of plant
items.why: Fungi are our close relatives, so their cells work much as ours do. A medicine that harms a fungus cell can easily harm our cells too. Bacteria are built very differently, so more medicines can hit them alone.

items.p: The passing of a gene to a neighbour who is not one's offspring is called ____ gene transfer.
items.why: Horizontal means sideways, from one being to another of the same generation. Passing genes to offspring is called vertical.

items.p: A lichen is a fungus and an alga in one body. Draw a lichen's place on a tree of life.
items.a: Answers vary. One good answer draws a line from the fungus twig and a line from the alga's twig that meet at one point marked 'lichen'.
items.why: No single tip of the tree fits a lichen. A strong drawing shows two twigs meeting, and so shows that a plain tree is not enough.
items.art: A tree of life with a twig labelled fungi and a twig labelled green algae on different branches, and empty space between them.

items.p: Put these events in the history of life in order, from the earliest to the latest.
a: Bacteria begin living inside another cell and become mitochondria
The first animals with many cells
items.why: Life began more than 3.5 billion years ago. The merger that gave mitochondria was about 2 billion years ago. Animals appear about 600 million years ago, and humans within the last few hundred thousand years.
items: The first animals with many cells
Bacteria begin living inside another cell and become mitochondria

items.p: A new microbe is known only from genes found in mud. What can scientists know about them, and what not?
items.a: They can know where the microbe sits on the tree of life, and guess from the genes what the microbe might feed on. They cannot know the shape of the cell, how they behave or whom they live with, until someone grows them and looks.
items.why: A strong answer separates what genes show directly, the family, from what must be seen in a living cell.

items.p: Why are viruses left off the usual tree of life?
opts: They share no gene with all cells
They are too small to study
They do not change over time
They are a kind of bacteria
items.why: The tree is built from genes that every cell has, such as ribosome genes. Viruses have no ribosomes and no such genes, so there is nothing to line up.

items.p: Match each living being to what makes them a hard case for sorting.
items.why: Each of these beings broke a sorting rule that people once trusted. Hard cases are where the rules get tested.
pairs: makes spores but is a giant creeping cell
two beings living as one body
looks like a plant, on another branch

items.p: Three of these pairs are close relatives. Which pair only look alike?
items.why: Water moulds grow in threads like fungi, but their genes place them with the brown seaweeds. The other three pairs share recent ancestors.

items.p: On a drawing of a plant cell, label the three parts that carry DNA from three different lines of ancestors.
a: The nucleus: DNA of the cell's own line
A mitochondrion: DNA descended from bacteria
A chloroplast: DNA descended from cyanobacteria
items.why: A plant cell is a merger of three lines. Each of the three parts still keeps some DNA of their own.
items.art: A box-shaped plant cell with a large round part, several small bean-shaped parts and several green oval parts, with three blank label lines.

quiz.p: Which of these living beings has a cell with no nucleus?
quiz.why: Bacteria have no nucleus. Yeast, amoebae and mosses are eukaryotes, so their cells have one. Choosing yeast or amoeba mixes up 'one cell' with 'no nucleus'.

quiz.p: How does a fungus get food?
opts: Digests it outside and soaks it up
quiz.why: A fungus lets digesting juices out onto food and soaks up the result. 'Makes it from light' treats a fungus as a plant, which was the mistake of two hundred years.

quiz.p: Which two kingdoms are each other's closest relatives?
quiz.why: Gene studies since 1993 put fungi and animals together. Choosing fungi and plants goes by looks: both stand still.

quiz.p: What first showed that archaea are not bacteria?
opts: Their ribosome gene was very different
quiz.why: In 1977 Carl Woese and George Fox found that the ribosome gene of methane-makers was as far from bacteria's as from ours. Archaea are the same size as bacteria and have no nucleus.

quiz.p: True or false: every living being is either a plant or an animal.
quiz.why: False. Fungi, protists, bacteria and archaea are neither. The two-kingdom idea lasted until microscopes showed beings who fitted neither box.

quiz.p: Two beings differ in very few letters of the same gene. What does that suggest?
quiz.why: Differences build up over time. Few differences mean that little time has passed since the two were one family.

quiz.p: Why do scientists say that protists are not one family?
opts: They sit on many separate branches
quiz.why: Protists are every eukaryote who is not an animal, a plant or a fungus. Some are nearer to animals, and some nearer to plants. Many are not parasites, and some are large seaweeds.

quiz.p: Where did the mitochondria in your cells come from?
opts: Bacteria who lived inside another cell
quiz.why: Mitochondria are descended from bacteria who began living inside another cell about two billion years ago. They still have a little DNA of their own, which matches bacteria.

quiz.p: Which of these do scientists still argue about today?
opts: Whether life has two domains or three
quiz.why: Some gene trees put our branch beside the archaea, which gives three domains. Others put our branch inside the archaea, which gives two. The other three are settled.

quiz.p: Which living beings have the most branches on the tree of life?
quiz.why: Life was only microbes for most of its history, so microbes have had the longest time to branch. Animals look many to us because we can see them.

quiz.p: A being has many cells with no cell walls, and takes food inside the body. Which group?
quiz.why: Many cells, no cell walls and food taken inside the body are the marks of an animal. Fungi and plants have cell walls, and a bacterium is a single cell.

quiz.p: True or false: scientists found the number of kingdoms by measuring.
quiz.why: False. Measuring shows who is related to whom. The number of kingdoms depends on where people choose to draw the lines, which is why books give five, six or seven.

applications: Choosing a medicine. A doctor must know whether an illness is caused by a bacterium, a fungus, a protist or a virus. Antibiotics act only on bacteria. Malaria is caused by a protist and needs different medicines.
Naming an unknown microbe. Hospital and water-testing laboratories read the ribosome gene of a microbe and compare it with known ones, as Carl Woese did.
Biogas. A gobar gas plant keeps air out of the tank, because the archaea who make methane live only where there is no oxygen.
Food. Bakers use a fungus, yeast. Curd is made by bacteria. Idli batter is raised by bacteria and yeasts together. Mushroom growers feed a fungus on straw.
Finding medicines. Penicillin comes from a mould, a fungus, and kills bacteria. Knowing who is related to whom tells scientists where to look for similar chemicals.
Farming. Bacteria living in the root lumps of groundnut and pulse plants take nitrogen from the air. Farmers add these bacteria to seeds as biofertiliser.
Looking for life on other worlds. Scientists know what all life on Earth shares, so they can ask whether something found elsewhere belongs to our tree.

open_questions.q: Does life have two first branches or three?
open_questions.why_open: The split is about two billion years old, and gene trees of events that old change with the genes and methods used. Few of the key archaea have been grown and watched alive.

open_questions.q: How did the first cell with a nucleus come about?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists agree that an archaeon-like cell and a bacterium merged. They do not agree on how the two first came to live together, or whether the nucleus came before or after.

open_questions.q: How many kinds of microbes are there?
open_questions.why_open: Estimates run from a few million to a million million. Most microbes cannot yet be grown, and scientists do not agree on what counts as one 'kind' of bacterium.

open_questions.q: Where did viruses come from, and how should a picture of life's history show them?
open_questions.why_open: Viruses share no gene with all cells, and they probably arose more than once. Nobody has found a way to draw them that everyone accepts.

open_questions.q: Is all life on Earth on one tree?
open_questions.why_open: Every being studied so far uses the same code. But most microbes have never been studied, and a few scientists have asked whether a second kind of life could be here unnoticed. Nobody has found one.

open_questions.q: Does a single cell experience anything?
open_questions.why_open: Bacteria, archaea and protists sense, signal and choose. Nobody knows how to test whether anything like awareness goes with that.

maths.problem: In the Weight of Life, plants took 450 millimetres of a strip 550 millimetres long. What percentage of the weight of all life is plants? Round to the nearest whole number.
maths.explain: Divide the part by the whole: 450 ÷ 550 = 0.818. Multiply by 100 to get 81.8 percent, which rounds to 82 percent. So more than four fifths of the weight of life is plants.
maths.context: This is about the Weight of Life, where you marked a paper strip with a length for each big group of living beings.
maths.why_maths: A strip shows that plants are the biggest part. A percentage says how big, in a way you can compare with other figures.

maths.problem: In the Weight of Life, all fungi were 12 millimetres on the strip and all humans were 0.06 of a millimetre. How many times as heavy as all humans are all fungi?
maths.explain: Divide the larger by the smaller: 12 ÷ 0.06. Multiply both by 100 to remove the decimal: 1,200 ÷ 6 = 200. So the fungi of the world weigh about 200 times as much as all the people.
maths.context: This is about the Weight of Life, where one millimetre of paper strip stood for one billion tonnes of carbon in living beings.
maths.why_maths: Nobody can picture 0.06 of a millimetre. Dividing turns two awkward numbers into one plain comparison.

maths.problem: In the Hidden Tree Test, 4 beings gave 6 pairs to compare. How many pairs would 5 beings give? How many would 6 give, and 10? Find the rule.
maths.answer: 5 beings give 10 pairs, 6 give 15 and 10 give 45.
maths.explain: Each new being must be compared with all the earlier ones. So the fifth being adds 4 pairs: 6 + 4 = 10. The sixth adds 5: 10 + 5 = 15. Going on, 21, 28, 36 and then 45 for 10 beings. The rule is: multiply the number of beings by one less, and halve it. For 10 beings, 10 × 9 ÷ 2 = 45.
maths.context: This is about the Hidden Tree Test, where you counted the letters that differ between every pair of four beings.
maths.why_maths: The number of pairs grows much faster than the number of beings. This is why scientists who compare thousands of beings need computers.

maths.problem: In a hidden tree, every copy gets 2 changed letters and no place changes twice. Two beings differ in 12 letters. How many copyings ago did they share an ancestor?
maths.explain: After the two lines part, each line gets 2 new changes at every copying. So the two beings move apart by 2 + 2 = 4 letters at every copying. 12 ÷ 4 = 3. They shared an ancestor 3 copyings ago.
maths.context: This is about the Hidden Tree Test, where each copied message had exactly two letters changed.
maths.why_maths: If changes come at a steady rate, the count of differences works as a clock. Scientists use this to estimate how long ago two groups of living beings split.

maths.problem: A key says: 'If a being is a plant, then their cells have a nucleus.' A brown seaweed has cells with a nucleus. Does it follow that a brown seaweed is a plant?
maths.explain: The rule runs one way only. Every plant has a nucleus, but so do amoebae, mushrooms and humans. Knowing that a being has a nucleus tells you only that the rule has not ruled them out. A brown seaweed is in fact a protist.
maths.context: This is about Six Questions, where you wrote a key of yes-or-no questions for the big groups of life.
maths.why_maths: A key is a chain of if-then rules. Reading a rule backwards is the commonest mistake in using one, and logic shows why it fails.

maths.problem: Life is at least 3,500 million years old. Animals appear about 600 million years ago. A 35 centimetre line stands for all of that time. How long is the part with animals in it? What fraction of the line had only single cells and simple colonies?
maths.answer: The part with animals is 6 centimetres long. About 29 of the 35 centimetres, or roughly five sixths, came before animals.
maths.explain: 35 centimetres stand for 3,500 million years, so 1 centimetre stands for 100 million years. 600 ÷ 100 = 6 centimetres. 35 − 6 = 29 centimetres came before animals. 29 ÷ 35 is about 0.83, which is close to five sixths.
maths.context: This is about A Fair Tree for the Wall, where one rule was to share the poster by how old each branch is.
maths.why_maths: Numbers in millions of years are hard to compare. A line drawn to scale shows at a glance how late animals arrived.

warmup.q: Name the three domains of life.
What does a eukaryote cell have that a bacterium does not?

warmup.a: They digest food outside their body and soak it up.

warmup.q: Which kingdom is the closest relative of the animals?
Who makes the gas in a gobar gas plant?
Is 'protist' one family or a label for leftovers?
warmup.a: A label for every eukaryote who is not an animal, a plant or a fungus.

warmup.q: Two beings differ in very few gene letters. What does that tell you?
warmup.a: They shared an ancestor not long ago.

warmup.q: Where did your mitochondria come from?
warmup.a: From bacteria who began living inside another cell.

playtest: Every part was reasoned through step by step as a family in a city flat would do it. None has yet been tried at home, so please treat amounts and times as a starting point. The Hidden Tree Test (the main investigation) needs only paper, a pencil and scissors. The ready-made messages were checked by computer: sisters differ in 4 letters and the other pairs in 8. With a home-made tree the same counts come out, as long as no chit is put back and exactly two letters change in each copy. The grown-up needs about eight minutes alone to build the tree, and must keep the three hidden slips out of sight. A child working alone uses the ready-made messages, so the surprise is smaller. Light or Dark takes a week. Chapati or roti usually shows mould in three to seven days, and packet bread can take longer because it has preservatives. In a dry or cold room, allow three more days. Keep both sets out of direct sun, or the test is not fair. Never open a mouldy pouch. Which Kingdom? and Closer Relative? were played through on paper for one, two and four players. Six Questions needs the cards from Which Kingdom?. The Weight of Life needs a ruler marked in millimetres. A Census of Our Home works without a hand lens, and a grown-up goes along for the search outside. Nothing in the core path needs a garden. Facts that were looked up while writing: the figures for the weight of life (Bar-On and others, 2018), the papers and dates of Whittaker, Woese, Baldauf and Palmer, Spang, Imachi and Hug, the 2024 estimate for the age of the last shared ancestor, the counts of named and estimated species, the salt-pan archaea of Goa and Tamil Nadu, the steps of oyster mushroom growing, and the three video addresses. The films were not watched. Facts written from general knowledge and not looked up this time, which a person may wish to check: that Robert Whittaker left brown seaweeds in the plant kingdom in 1969, the dates for Chatton, Stanier and van Niel, Hennig, Margulis, Doolittle and Nakagaki, the date of about 600 million years for the first animals, and the verse numbers of the Tolkappiyam passage, which differ between editions.
